The starting condition was worse than the plan recorded: of the six scalars the plan asked to replace, **four — `MediaTopologyId`, `ConferenceId`, `SupervisorAgentId`, `SupervisorLegId` — were never written by any code path in the product.** Only `CallSessionStore.ValidateTopology` read them. So the practical consequence was not that supervisor state was modelled badly, it was that **supervisor monitoring had no durable state at all**: `ContactCenterMonitoringService` fired a provider command, published an event, and left nothing behind. Nothing could report that a supervisor was listening, refuse a second engagement by the same supervisor, or release the correct leg when one of two engagements stopped. `CallSession` now carries `Legs` (role + normalized `CallLegStatus` + address + agent + started/answered/ended + hangup cause), a `Bridge` whose `Participants` record `JoinedUtc` and `LeftUtc` instead of being removed, `Consults`, `MonitorSessions`, and typed `Relationships`; `IsConference`, `ParticipantCount` and `ActiveMonitorSessions` are `[JsonIgnore]` computed views. `CallTopologyProjector` is the sole writer. `InteractionCallLeg.Status` is now the `CallLegStatus` enum instead of a string. Because membership is append-only, `Bridge.ParticipantsAt(instant)` reconstructs who was on the call at a past moment — the plan's first exit criterion — and that is only meaningful because leaving stamps a time rather than deleting the entry. `Bridge.ReportedParticipantCount` is kept **separate** from observed membership deliberately: a provider that publishes only a count cannot say who those parties are, and fabricating members to match the count would turn membership history into fiction, so the count wins for display while membership stays factual. `EndLeg` sets `Failed` when the leg never answered and `Ended` when it did, which is what lets abandon and no-answer reporting separate without provider vocabulary. Consultative transfers record a `ConsultCall` plus a `CallRelationship` (second exit criterion), and an ended consult ends its leg and releases its membership so no leg is left dangling. Monitor, whisper and barge each record a `MonitorSession`, with barge alone joining the supervisor to the bridge because barge puts the supervisor in the conversation while the other two do not (third exit criterion); a second engagement by the same supervisor on the same call is refused, because two engagements by one supervisor are indistinguishable and a later stop would release an arbitrary one and leave the other listening. `AsteriskContactCenterVoiceProvider` now populates the neutral `ContactCenterVoiceProviderResult.ProviderLegId` on connect, transfer and monitoring results, and `AnswerProviderCommandTypeExecutor` uses it to join the agent leg to the bridge, so the agent is a real party rather than a name on the session. This respects W1.6: `ProviderVoiceEvent` already declared `ProviderLegId`, so no vendor vocabulary was added to the neutral contract. **A sabotage probe found a real hole in the gate and it was fixed rather than explained away.** The first version of the source scan classified the receiver by written type, mirroring the W2.1 scan. Probe P8 added `callSession.Legs.Add(...)` to `ContactCenterTransferService` and the gate **passed** — the receiver came from `var callSession = await manager.FindByInteractionIdAsync(...)`, so there was no written type to recognize. The scan was rewritten to match on member name alone, which is sound only while those names belong to exactly one type, so a companion case `TheTopologyMemberNames_AreUniqueToTheCallSession` pins that each of `Legs`, `Bridge`, `Consults`, `MonitorSessions`, `Relationships` is declared exactly once across the scanned projects and fails if that stops being true. `Participants` is *not* matched by name because `Interaction` also declares it; it counts only when reached through `.Bridge`. P8 re-run against the hardened scan fails as it should. Falsified with 9 probes (a 10th, aimed at the discarded receiver-typing helper, became obsolete when that helper was deleted and is not counted): erasing the participant on leave (2 fail), collapsing `EndLeg` to always `Ended` (1), allowing duplicate relationship edges (1), accepting a relationship with no identifier (1), leaving an ended consult's leg open (1), reintroducing a `ConferenceId` scalar on `CallSession` (1), blinding the scan's member matching (1), adding a topology write outside the projector (1), and declaring a topology member name on a second type (1) — each fails only the intended assertions. **Deviations recorded rather than hidden.** (1) A provider that reports no leg identifier for a supervisor engagement still produces a `MonitorSession` with a null `ProviderLegId`: the engagement is on the record, but a barge cannot place the supervisor on the bridge without a leg to place. (2) `CallConferenceChanged` was previously raised on *any* participant-count change; because the count was never written it never fired for a bridge change, and now that it is real it would fire on ordinary two-party setup, so the event is scoped to calls that are or have just stopped being a conference. The two existing conference cases in `ProviderVoiceEventServiceTests` still assert it fires for real conference changes. (3) The plan named the scalar `BridgeId`; W1.6 had already renamed it `MediaTopologyId`, and that is the field this item removed. **A second review pass found six defects in the first implementation; all six were fixed and pinned, not argued away.** (a) *Critical.* No provider populates `ProviderVoiceEvent.ProviderLegId`, so ingestion always addressed the leg named by `ProviderCallId` — the customer channel — while `AnswerProviderCommandTypeExecutor` recorded the agent leg under a different identifier. The hangup ended only the customer leg, the `DestroyBridge` guard `Legs.All(l => l.EndedUtc.HasValue)` was therefore never satisfied, and because a terminal session discards every later delivery nothing could ever repair it: every completed call kept the agent joined to the bridge forever, which defeats the reconstruction guarantee this item exists to provide. Terminal handling now calls a new `CallTopologyProjector.EndRemainingLegs` and destroys the bridge unconditionally. (b) *Critical.* `EndLeg` stamped `EndedUtc` with no clamp while `CallSessionStore.ValidateTopology` rejects `EndedUtc < StartedUtc`. `VoiceStreamOrdering` deliberately exempts terminal deliveries from its timestamp guard precisely because a hangup can carry a timestamp behind the state change before it, and the two writers mix clock domains (`AnswerProviderCommandTypeExecutor` stamps the start from `IClock`, ingestion stamps the end from the provider's `OccurredUtc`). The resulting `InvalidOperationException` is not retried by `IngestAsync`, so the webhook would 500 deterministically forever and the call would stay `Connected` with its agent occupied. `EndLeg` now clamps exactly as `Leave` and `DestroyBridge` already did. (c) *High.* `MonitorSession.SupervisorAgentId` was written with a **user** identifier (`ClaimTypes.NameIdentifier`) while `TargetAgentId` held an agent-profile identifier, so the store's self-monitoring guard compared two identity spaces and could never fire, and a barge put a user identifier in `BridgeParticipant.AgentId` next to agent-profile identifiers. `MonitorSession` now records `SupervisorUserId` and `SupervisorAgentId` separately; engagements are matched on the user identifier (always present) and the self-monitoring invariant compares agent identifiers only. (d) `EnsureBridge` with a changed provider bridge identifier called `DestroyBridge` but never cleared `session.Bridge`, so it returned the destroyed bridge under the old identifier; the next `Join` would then violate the store's "a destroyed bridge cannot retain a participant that never left" invariant. The previous bridge is now retained in `CallSession.PriorBridges` and a fresh one created, and `CallSession.ParticipantsAt` searches all of them so the move does not erase history. (e) `CallLeg.HangupCause` was always null, because `ApplyProviderDetails` runs before `ApplyHangupCause` and read `session.HangupCause` while it was still unassigned. It now reads the delivery's own cause. Chasing that uncovered a further pre-existing defect: `CloneProviderEvent` silently dropped `HangupCause`, so a cause the provider genuinely reported was replaced by one inferred from the call state, with nothing to indicate the real one had been lost. A new `ProviderVoiceEventCloneCompletenessTests` compares the clone's initializer against the type's settable properties by reflection so any future field the copy forgets fails the build. (W10.5 later removed the clone entirely by making the event immutable, and replaced that test with `ProviderVoiceEventImmutabilityTests`.) (f) The `TransferredTo` relationship was never recorded, because Asterisk's `TransferSuccess` set `ProviderLegId` but not `ProviderCallId` and `Relate` short-circuits when every identifier is null — the transfer-chain feature was dead for the only shipped voice provider. **The same review demonstrated four ways to mutate topology past the name-based scan, and the scan was hardened against all four rather than documented around them:** aliasing the collection into a local first (`var legs = callSession.Legs`), mutating objects reached *through* a topology member (`callSession.Bridge.DestroyedUtc = …`, `callSession.Legs[0].Status = …`), seeding topology inside an object initializer, and using a mutator absent from the listed set. The scan now treats any expression whose left spine reaches a topology member as topology, flags aliasing and hand-off of a member, flags initializer seeding, and recognizes *reads* through an allow list so an unfamiliar method counts as a mutation instead of being ignored. A further case, `EveryProjectThatCanSeeTheCallSession_IsScannedByTheAuthorityGate`, fails if a project that references the Contact Center core is not in the scanned folder list — closing the reviewer's observation that the folder list was complete only by accident. Eleven further probes falsify the corrected work: the four evasions above (4 fail), an unlisted mutator (1), removing `EndRemainingLegs` (1), removing the `EndLeg` clamp (1), removing the bridge rotation (2), collapsing the supervisor identifiers back into one field (1), dropping `HangupCause` from the clone (1), and removing a referencing project from the scanned list (1).  **A third pass reviewed the fixes themselves and found four more, all fixed.** (g) *High, and caused by fix (a).* Destroying the bridge on every terminal delivery meant every ended call now has a destroyed bridge, and `Join` refused only a *missing* bridge, not a destroyed one. `AnswerProviderCommandTypeExecutor.ProjectSuccessAsync` runs **after** the provider round-trip that connects the agent and had no state guard, so a caller hanging up mid-connect would add a live participant to a closed bridge, `ValidateBridge` would throw inside `UpdateAsync`, and the accept would fail with an unhandled error leaving the durable command unsettled. `Join` now refuses a destroyed bridge and the executor skips topology projection on a terminal session — the guard and the belt, because either alone leaves the other path open. (h) Ending a call closed its legs and bridge but never its supervisor engagements, and stopping an engagement is refused once the call is terminal, so an engagement live at hangup could never be closed by anyone: the session went on reporting a supervisor as listening while their leg was ended and their membership released, a record that contradicts itself. `EndRemainingMonitorSessions` closes them with the call. (i) Fix (c) made the self-monitoring guard *able* to fire for the first time, and it fired at persist time — after `EngageAsync` had already brought up a real snoop or barge channel — so the first supervisor to try monitoring their own call would get a 500 and an orphaned provider leg nothing could later stop. The refusal moved ahead of the provider command. (j) The hardened scan still had three one-line evasions, each breaking the left spine a different way: a `foreach` variable is not a declarator, so iterating the collection handed out every element unrooted; an element accessor on the read allow list (`First`, `Single`, …) handed out a mutable object the scan then stopped tracking; and `TopologyMemberAccessName` unwrapped parentheses and `!` but not `?.`, so `var bridge = session?.Bridge` was not aliasing. All three are closed. Closing them naively reported `CallSessionStore.ValidateTopology`, which iterates topology purely to validate it — a false positive of exactly the kind that gets a gate weakened later — so aliasing is now reported only when the alias is **written through, called with an unlisted member, or handed to something that could mutate it**, following a hand-off one call deep into a same-file method so a mutation moved behind a helper is still found. Passing a *field* of an alias is not a hand-off, because that passes a copy of the value. Separately, `EveryProjectThatCanSeeTheCallSession_IsScannedByTheAuthorityGate` matched only **direct** references; it now walks the whole `ProjectReference` closure, which immediately proved the point by naming three unscanned projects that reach `CallSession` transitively through the Contact Center module — `Cms.Core.Targets`, `Aspire.AppHost` and `Cms.Web` — all now scanned. Eight further probes falsify this round: the three evasions (1 fail each), removing the destroyed-bridge `Join` guard (1), removing `EndRemainingMonitorSessions` (1), removing the executor's terminal guard (1), removing the pre-flight self-monitor refusal (1), and dropping a newly scanned project from the folder list (1). **Deviation recorded rather than hidden:** the bridge-rotation path from fix (d) is correct and tested but unreachable in production, because no contract carries a provider media-topology identifier — W1.6 deliberately made bridge identifiers provider-private — so every call's bridge has a null `ProviderBridgeId` and `PriorBridges` is always empty outside tests. The retention of a prior bridge becomes live the moment a provider reports one; until then a provider that moves the parties to different media still silently keeps the old bridge object. Total for this item: **28 falsifying probes.** Re-verified after the fixes: full suite 3,005 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped, activation 41 passed / 0 failed / 2 skipped, distributed 12 passed with the one known Redis failure, strict Release build 0 warnings / 0 errors, docs build succeeded.

### Wave 3 — Data lifecycle
- [x] W2.3 Retention `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test` (`CC-D014`) — `ContactCenterRetentionCoverageTests` (15 executed cases) plus `ContactCenterRetentionPersistenceTests` (5) and the rewritten `ContactCenterRetentionServiceTests` (8); full suite 3,034 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped (3m43s), activation 41 passed / 0 failed / 2 skipped, distributed 12 passed / 1 failed (the Redis-backplane case, which requires `CONTACT_CENTER_REDIS_CONFIGURATION` and is unavailable locally). Retention purged `InteractionEvent` and nothing else, so twelve tables that grow with traffic had no policy at all — a gap that stays invisible until an operator runs out of disk, because nothing anywhere states that a table is meant to be bounded. Each entity now declares a policy naming the timestamp it ages from, what makes one of its records finished, and which floors hold it beyond its window, and twelve of them were added: `Interaction`, `CallSession`, `QueueItem`, `ActivityReservation`, `ContactCenterOutboxMessage`, `ProviderWebhookInboxMessage`, `ProviderCommand`, `AgentSession`, `ContactCenterEventMetric`, `ContactCenterProcessedEvent`, `CallbackRequest`, and the pre-existing `InteractionEvent` moved onto the same footing. Seven indexes had no timestamp that could age them at all and gained one. The choice of timestamp is the substance of the work item rather than a detail: a record is aged from when it *settled*, never from when it arrived, was last retried, or was scheduled. Ageing a queue item from `EnqueuedUtc` would shorten the window in proportion to how long the caller waited and so delete exactly the worst-wait records an operator needs to explain what went wrong; ageing a provider command from `NextAttemptUtc` follows a value that keeps moving during backoff; ageing a callback from `ScheduledUtc` reaches a date weeks in the future. Each new column is backfilled in one set-based statement, and both directions of getting that wrong are real: a non-nullable timestamp added without a backfill leaves every existing row at `DateTime.MinValue` — older than any cutoff — and the first cycle after an upgrade would empty the table, which for processed-event markers silently reintroduces duplicate side effects; while a *nullable* timestamp added without a backfill leaves every pre-upgrade row null, and because every predicate begins by rejecting nulls the entire legacy backlog would be immortal while the cycle reported success. The backfill dates legacy rows from the upgrade, which is later than the truth and so can only delay a purge rather than bring one forward, and is restricted to rows already in a settled status so nothing in flight is handed a false completion time. That is now enforced: an upgrade step that adds a settlement column and does not backfill it fails the build. Floors are scoped rather than global: legal hold holds communication history, the replay horizon holds only the event log projections replay from, and a new redelivery envelope holds deduplication markers, whose premature deletion makes a redelivered event look new. The service drains each entity across batches until its table is empty instead of truncating at a fixed batch count as it silently did before, commits between batches so a large drain is not one unbounded transaction, isolates a failing entity so one unhealthy table cannot keep every other table growing, and reports remaining work when its budget runs out. Two of the nine sabotage probes were initially *not* caught and forced the gates to be strengthened: purging provider commands by their retry time instead of their completion time passed, because the status guard still protected the live rows; and dropping the replay horizon from the event log passed, because the legal-hold floor was the larger of the two and hid it. The suite now pins the settlement column per entity and asserts the floors under two configurations that swap which floor dominates. The claimed exit condition is met by proof rather than by scale: a 5-million-row cycle is expressed as the default batch size times the per-cycle budget, and the honest CI substitute is a real SQLite database where a backlog larger than one batch drains within a single cycle, an exhausted budget is reported rather than looking like success, and — the assertion that actually matters — the survivors are checked by name, because a subtly wrong predicate still deletes a plausible number of rows. The feature-activation audit then found the defect that would have made all of it inert: every policy was registered in the base feature, whose dependency closure does not contain the queue, reservation, callback, provider-command, webhook-inbox or agent-session stores, so on a real tenant the retention service could not be constructed at all and *nothing* would have been purged, including the one table that was already working. Each policy now registers in the feature that owns its store. "No table lacks a policy" is enforced by reflecting over every index and requiring a registered policy or a written exemption, so the ten exempted tables (configuration, reference data and projection checkpoints) are recorded decisions rather than omissions. Review then falsified two of those decisions and both were fixed rather than argued. The reservation policy treated `Accepted` as settled, but accepting *is* the live claim an agent holds — deleting one releases the unique activity claim so the same work can be reserved twice, and strips the agent's own assignment out from under them; the terminal set is now rejected, expired or canceled, aged from `ModifiedUtc` rather than from creation. And the work-state exemption described a lifecycle that does not exist: nothing anywhere deletes a work state, so that table grew by a row for every activity ever routed. It now has a policy, aged by last mutation alone because closure is owned by the CRM activity, which is safe only because a missing work state is recreated and re-seeded from the activity projection on next access — the same adoption path W2.1 designed for pre-existing tenants. Two further gates came out of that review: a policy may only treat statuses declared terminal *by name* as expired, so widening one to a live status fails the build; and the batch budget is spent per entity, because a shared budget let whichever policy ran first consume the whole cycle and leave every entity behind it permanently untouched. Six further sabotage probes were run against the strengthened gates and all six were caught. A second review then found the defect that would have made two of the new policies inert in exactly the way the work item exists to prevent: `ActivityReservation` and `CallbackRequest` are aged from their modification time, and *nothing wrote it* — the catalog manager does not stamp it and no handler fires on the programmatic update path these services use — so both policies matched no row at all while their entities reported themselves drained every cycle. The same review found the callback policy could not have matched anyway, because no code path ever set a callback to `Completed`, `Canceled` or `Failed`; those statuses exist but are unreachable. Both are fixed at the writer rather than at the predicate: the reservation service stamps the settlement time on every release and cancellation, the dialer stamps it when a callback is promoted, and a callback counts as settled once it is scheduled, because from that point the promoted activity is the durable record. A ninth gate now asserts that every settlement column an active policy reads is written somewhere outside the index projection, so a column that nothing produces cannot be introduced again, and two further probes — removing the reservation stamp and removing the callback stamp — were both caught. A third review then falsified that gate itself: matching a file that mentions the model and contains the column assignment anywhere was satisfied by an unrelated assignment, and the very fix for the reservation defect was what made the work-state case pass, so deleting the one statement that stamps a work state would have left the suite green. The gate now names the production statement on each settlement path, and removing the work-state stamp is caught. The same review found the webhook inbox aged from receipt with no redelivery floor, which is the one place in the set that broke the work item's own rule: a completed inbox row is the tombstone that makes a repeated provider delivery a duplicate — its payload is cleared at settlement and it is kept for nothing else — so ageing it from receipt shortened the deduplication guarantee by the whole retry envelope, and any window below the envelope let a redelivered webhook re-run its side effect and re-create an interaction retention had already deleted. It is now aged from settlement, stamped on completion and on dead-lettering, and floored by the redelivery envelope. Two gates were degenerate and were rewritten: the liveness check accepted any nullable member, so the two policies it was named for passed without testing a status at all; it now requires a status test wherever a finished state is declared and requires the settlement column itself to be absent while a record is live where none is. And five predicates had no covering index, so at steady state each terminating batch was a full scan of the largest tables in the schema on every cycle — the exact condition the 5-million-row exit criterion is about; those indexes were added and a gate now requires one per policy. Purged counts are now recorded only after the deletes commit, and a cycle stopped by a failed commit marks the entities it never reached as unfinished so an untouched backlog is not indistinguishable from a drained one. Three further probes were run and all three were caught. A fourth review found the last way a correct policy can still be inert, and it is not in the policy at all: the upgrade step that backfills the webhook settlement column quoted an identifier with a hardcoded double quote, and on an engine that reads that quote as a string literal the filter compares the constant text to two status numbers, matches nothing, and the backfill reports success having touched no rows — so every pre-upgrade row stays null, every predicate rejects nulls, and the entire legacy backlog is immortal while the cycle reports the entity drained. The existing backfill gate could not have caught it, because it checks that a backfill exists and names the right column, not that the statement can execute meaningfully anywhere; a fifteenth gate now requires every migration that writes raw SQL to take its identifiers from the dialect, and the probe that reinstates the hardcoded quote is caught. The same review corrected three narrower claims: the webhook floor now derives from the seven-day tombstone horizon the inbox itself enforces rather than from a delivery-envelope setting nothing in the product configures, so the floor is real by default rather than nominally present and zero; the promoted activity now carries the callback's notes, because the callback policy justifies its purge by asserting the activity is the durable record and that was not true of everything the callback held; and an entity whose purging is disabled is no longer reported as unfinished, which had made a deliberately retained table indistinguishable from a backlog the cycle ran out of budget to drain. A fifth review found three more, all of the same shape — a guarantee that is stated but not actually enforced. The settlement-writer gate matched its declared assignment anywhere in the declaring file, and a type usually has several settlement methods, so deleting the stamp from the one path that produces a status no other method produces left the whole suite green: removing it from the provider-command failure path made every failed command immortal without a single test noticing. The gate now locates the assignment inside the named method that owns each settlement path, and the probe that deletes the failure-path stamp is caught. The webhook inbox turned out to be purged twice — the new policy and the pre-existing tombstone sweep both delete settled rows — so the shorter of the two decided the real window and the sweep, holding a compiled seven-day constant, always won: `WebhookInboxMessageRetentionDays` was an operator setting that did nothing at all for completed rows, which are almost the entire table. The two are now reconciled in both directions, the policy never deleting inside the duplicate-detection horizon and the sweep never deleting before the configured window. And the drain loop's claim to isolate a failing entity was only half true: deletes are staged into one session shared by every entity, so a batch that failed partway through left its staged deletes to be committed by the next entity's flush, under that entity's transaction and counted against nobody. A failed batch now reports what it staged, and the cycle commits and attributes it before moving on. Three further probes were run and all three were caught.
- [x] W2.4 Query plans `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test` + `contact_center_operations_gates.yml#redis-backplane-two-node` (`CC-D015`) — `InteractionQueryPlanBudgetTests` (4 executed cases, SQLite `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`, covering both the hand-written statement and the pipeline-generated reservation queries), `InteractionPostgresQueryPlanBudgetTests` (2 executed cases against a real PostgreSQL service — a plan budget and an execution test), and a new `AvailabilityStoreSharedDatabaseTests` case for same-unit-of-work visibility; full suite 3,039 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped, activation 41 passed / 0 failed / 2 skipped, distributed 14 passed / 1 failed (the Redis-backplane case, which requires `CONTACT_CENTER_REDIS_CONFIGURATION` and is unavailable locally). W2.3 bounded how large the tables get; this bounds how much of them a query reads, and the distinction matters because the two failures do not look alike. A table that grows without limit eventually fills a disk and announces itself. A query that reads a whole table returns exactly the right answer every single time and simply gets slower in proportion to how much history the tenant has accumulated, so there is no functional test anywhere that can see it — only the plan is evidence, which is why the exit criterion is an `EXPLAIN` budget rather than a latency number. The statement chosen is the one routing runs before every offer: how much live work each candidate agent already holds. It was wrong in three independent ways at once. Its predicate was a chain of inequalities — not ended, not failed, not created — which an index cannot satisfy, because an index orders values and an inequality does not name the ones it wants; its results were materialized one row per interaction and grouped in memory, so the cost of a routing decision scaled with how busy the contact center was, which is precisely when a routing decision must be cheapest; and the only composite index on the table leads with `DocumentId`, the YesSql join key, which serves join-back and delete-by-document and answers nothing whatsoever about an agent. All three are fixed together because fixing any one alone changes nothing: a sargable predicate with no index to seek still scans, an index with a non-sargable predicate is never used, and a database-side `GROUP BY` over a full scan is a full scan. The predicate is now an inclusive `Status IN (…)` over named status sets, the count is a SQL `GROUP BY`, and `IDX_InteractionIndex_ActiveByAgent (AgentId, Status, DocumentId)` is added *alongside* the existing indexes rather than replacing them, exactly as the work item requires, so it covers the count outright and the number is produced without touching the table. Making the predicate inclusive introduces a hazard the exclusive form did not have, and it is the more dangerous of the two: a status added to the enum later silently falls out of "occupying an agent", so an agent genuinely holding work in the new status reads as idle and is handed more — a routing defect that presents as an overloaded agent, not as an error. A gate therefore requires the declared sets to partition `InteractionStatus` exactly, so adding a status fails the build until someone classifies it. The statement is hand-written, which creates two further ways to be wrong, and both are gated rather than asserted in prose. It runs on the calling session's own transaction and flushes first, because a caller that reserves an interaction and then asks for that agent's load in the same unit of work must not be told the agent is free — that is precisely how an agent is handed a second interaction they are already handling; removing the flush is caught by a test that counts work written but not yet committed. And the text lives in one builder that both production and the gates read, so a gate cannot drift into proving a plan for a query nobody runs, while the schema under measurement is built by the shipped migrations rather than hand-copied, so it cannot prove a plan for indexes nobody deploys. Both engines are measured because the planners disagree while the results do not, and this was not theoretical: the first PostgreSQL run failed outright, and the cause was in the gate rather than the product — rewriting the bound agent list as a set-returning function gave the planner no row estimate and it fell back to a sequential scan, measuring a plan production never executes. Corrected to the per-element expansion the data provider actually emits, and seeded until the wanted rows are a small enough share of the table for the choice to be real, PostgreSQL seeks the index. The SQLite gate additionally requires both columns to be *seek constraints* rather than just naming the index, because an exclusive status chain still seeks by agent and then tests every interaction that agent has ever handled row by row: the plan names the index either way, and only the constraint list distinguishes bounded work from unbounded. Review then found the gate had a hole large enough to hide a statement that could not execute at all: both budgets rewrote the bound agent list into explicit placeholders before measuring, so they proved a plan for text production never sent, while the text production *did* send failed outright on PostgreSQL — the data-access layer expands a bound collection into placeholders only for providers without native array binding, and PostgreSQL is not one of them, so the count threw a syntax error on every call and agent selection was dead on the one engine this work item exists to protect. The statement now emits one numbered placeholder per agent from the shared builder, the rewriting was deleted so both gates measure the text verbatim, and a PostgreSQL gate now *executes* the store method and asserts the counts rather than only reading its plan, because a plan budget on an unexecutable statement is worse than no gate at all. Review also found the gated statement was not the reservation path: reservation counts live work through the query pipeline, not the hand-written statement, and reverting the pipeline predicate to the inequality chain left every new test green. A recording connection now captures the SQL the pipeline actually emits for both reservation queries and puts each under the same budget. Seven sabotage mutations were run — dropping the new index on SQLite and again on PostgreSQL, reverting the hand-written predicate to the inequality chain, removing the flush, leaving a status unclassified, restoring the collection binding, and reverting both pipeline predicates — and all seven were caught.
- [x] W2.5 Migration safety `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test` (`CC-D016`) — `OmnichannelActivitySchemaConvergenceTests` (3 executed cases), `MigrationStartupBudgetTests` (2 executed cases), and a new `InPlaceRebuild` justification in `MigrationAdditiveOnlyGuardTests`; full suite 3,045 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped. The work item names three defects and all three turned out to be understated. The two row-by-row backfills do not merely update one row at a time — each first reads the entire table into memory to detect duplicates, so a large tenant pays for the whole table twice, inside the transaction that gates its own startup. The plan proposes moving them to a batched background backfill; they were made set-based instead, which is strictly better, because a background backfill leaves a window in which the unique constraint the backfill exists to enable cannot yet be created, and the whole point of these two steps is to establish that constraint. Canonicalization is a lookup over a finite alias map, so the table is asked which aliases it actually holds and each is rewritten with one statement; the claim key is derived by the database from columns it already has, using the dialect's own concatenation because `||`, `+`, and `concat()` are not interchangeable across the four supported engines; and both in-memory duplicate scans became `GROUP BY … HAVING COUNT(*) > 1`, grouping by the composed key rather than by its parts so an upgrade rejects exactly the rows the unique index would later reject. The exit criterion asks that a tenant with a million activities activate within the startup budget. Wall-clock is the wrong instrument for that — it is dominated by the machine and would either flap in CI or be set so loose it proves nothing — so what is measured is whether the number of database round trips tracks the number of rows: the same migration runs against tenants that differ ten-fold in size and the statement counts must be equal. That gate was blind when first written, and the reason is worth recording: the recording connection returned the *inner* connection's transaction, so a caller working through `transaction.Connection` reached the unwrapped connection and every statement went unrecorded, reading as a passing budget rather than as a gate that sees nothing. The transaction is now wrapped too; with it wrapped, reverting one backfill to per-row shows 17 statements against 107. The third defect is six times wider than stated. It is not only `AssignmentStatus`: `Kind`, `AssignmentStatus`, `UrgencyLevel`, `Status`, and `InteractionType` are all declared `INT` on a fresh tenant and `TEXT` on an upgraded one, and `IDX_OmnichannelActivityMyActivities_DocumentId` is missing `AssignmentStatus` entirely on an upgraded tenant. It is invisible by construction: YesSql writes an enum as an integer whatever the column says, and SQLite's type affinity converts it on the way in and applies column affinity to comparisons, so an upgraded tenant behaves correctly on SQLite forever and fails only on an engine that does not coerce. No functional test can see this — only the declaration is evidence — which is why the gate compares `PRAGMA` output rather than query results. A prior session identified this exact divergence and deferred it because SQLite cannot `ALTER COLUMN`. That is true, and it is not the end of the matter: `DropIndex`, `AddColumn`, `DropColumn`, and `RenameColumn` all work, and add-copy-drop-rename produces a correctly typed column on every supported engine. The reconciliation therefore lives entirely in a new `UpdateFrom4Async`, leaving the historical steps untouched as this repository requires, so there is exactly one code path and the released `UpdateFrom1Async`/`UpdateFrom3Async` steps keep meaning what they meant when they shipped. Which historical schemas are reachable is decided by return value, not by source order, and the upgrade chain in the gate is walked the same way the host walks it, so a step no version can reach cannot be mistaken for one that runs — an initial reading that `UpdateFrom3Async` was dead code was wrong, and only walking by return value exposed that. The value translation matches both a member's number-as-text and its name, and falls through to `NULL`, so an unreadable legacy value is recorded as unknown rather than silently rewritten to the enum's first member, which would have been a data corruption disguised as a successful upgrade. The rebuild's removals are destructive, and rather than route them through the register's unchecked escape hatch a new machine-checked `InPlaceRebuild` justification was added: it requires the entry to name the operation that restores the object and then verifies that restoration is really present in the same migration step. Registering the new set-based helper also exposed a hole in the additive-only guard itself. It read the first argument of an execution call that reconstructed to anything, so a helper taking the schema builder before the statement had its *receiver* classified instead of its SQL, and a plain `UPDATE` was reported as unreadable — which, had it been waved through into the reviewed-dynamic-SQL register, would have permanently exempted call sites the gate can read perfectly well. It now classifies every argument and takes the most severe outcome, still falling back to the old behaviour when no argument carries readable text so a statement hidden in an unresolvable variable keeps failing closed. Five sabotage mutations were run — deleting one index recreation, removing the helper's rename, reverting each backfill to per-row, and turning one set-based statement destructive — and all five were caught. Review then raised the point that all of this was proven on the one engine whose type affinity is what hid the defect in the first place, and executing the upgrade against a real PostgreSQL instance found two further defects the SQLite gate could not see. First, version 4 is reachable in two different shapes — one whose enum columns are text and one whose enum columns are already correct — and running the text-to-number translation over an integer column coerces silently on SQLite and raises `42883` on PostgreSQL, so the rebuild now probes the column's declared type by reading an empty result set and returns without touching a column that is already right. Second, PostgreSQL and SQLite name only the index in a drop, so the name resolves against the connection's search path rather than the table's schema: a tenant whose tables live in a named schema drops nothing, and because the data layer writes the drop with `IF EXISTS` the miss is silent until the recreation reports `42P07` and the tenant cannot activate. The step now issues a schema-qualified drop first on exactly the engines whose own drop cannot find the index. A second review round then found that the qualified drop named the wrong index: the data layer prefixes index names on the engines that share one index namespace across tables and shortens names the engine cannot hold, so on a tenant with both a schema and a table prefix the qualified drop missed exactly as the unqualified one did. All three fixes are gated by `OmnichannelActivityPostgresMigrationTests`, which runs the upgrade against real PostgreSQL — with a schema and a table prefix both configured, because it is their combination that exposes the naming defect — from both reachable shapes, and all three were falsified by sabotage: removing the type probe reproduces `42883`, removing the qualified drop reproduces `42P07`, and dropping the prefix from the qualified name reproduces `42P07` against the prefixed index. The same round raised that the reconciliation was not resumable on MySQL, which commits each schema change on its own, so a single interrupted attempt would leave a tenant that can never activate: the replacement column is now added only when it is not already present, an attempt that stopped after the original column was dropped finishes by renaming the replacement rather than starting over and destroying the translated values, and the index drops are tolerant while the recreations are not, so a genuine failure is still reported. Authorizing that raw drop also strengthened the register: a removal written as SQL is reported by its leading verb rather than by an object name, so an in-place-rebuild entry for one must now name every object it takes away and each is checked for a matching recreation in the same step, which is stricter than trusting the verb; deleting any one of the three index recreations fails the build.

Docker is unavailable in this environment, so rather than hand-writing payloads and calling them recordings — which would have restated the implementation under a more credible name — the Asterisk project's own machine-readable REST Interface declarations for the pinned release (`22.10.1`) are vendored verbatim, behind a manifest recording the upstream repository, ref, URL and SHA-256 of each file plus the container tag and digest. The provenance suite recomputes those hashes and requires the vendored release to equal the release parsed out of the Asterisk `Dockerfile`, with exactly one vendored release directory, so an Asterisk version bump breaks the build — which is precisely what W5.4 asks for. The event suite scans the production mapper for the event types it interprets and requires the contract and cassettes to cover exactly that set, requires every property path the mapper depends on to resolve against the vendored declarations, requires every recorded payload to contain only fields those declarations permit, requires each tolerated compatibility fallback to stay absent from the corresponding model, and replays every cassette through the real mapper. The REST suite drives the real `AsteriskAriClient`, exercises all 17 methods `IAsteriskAriClient` publishes, and requires every issued request and query parameter to be declared by that release. The gates found two real product defects, both fixed here: channel variables were read from four locations, none of them `Channel.channelvars` — the only location the specification declares and a conforming Asterisk populates — so the interaction correlation id could never be recovered from a channel object; and recording duration was read from `StoredRecording`, which declares only a name and a format, so every completed recording reported no duration. - [x] W5.6 State machine property tests `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test` — `CallStateMachinePropertyTests` (9) — 8 executed properties plus a generator anti-vacuity property, 400 seeded delivery sequences each, 0 failed. W5.4 binds the providers to the protocol they speak; it says nothing about how that protocol is *delivered*. Provider nodes do not share a clock, do not sequence every event type, retry aggressively, reorder, and can report a call terminated more than once, and every pre-existing test of `ProviderVoiceEventService` exercised only the orderly case. The generator emits a real lifecycle and then corrupts its delivery with duplicates, whole-stream replays, Fisher-Yates reordering, +/-400ms clock skew against 250ms event spacing, streams where 40% of deliveries carry no sequence number, late backward state regressions stamped with the freshest timestamp *and* the highest sequence number so they reach the rank guard rather than dying at the staleness guards, and a second competing terminal that disagrees with the first. The properties drive the production `ProviderVoiceEventService` and the production `DefaultContactCenterEventPublisher` and require convergence to one terminal state and interaction status regardless of delivery order, no lifecycle-rank regression, no resurrection of a terminated call, no stranded call, no duplicated lifecycle domain event, and no live-only flag left set on a terminated call; a ninth property asserts anti-vacuity floors on the generator so the suite cannot decay into testing the orderly case again. The gates found two real product defects, both fixed here: a terminal delivery carrying a stale mute flag re-applied it *after* terminal normalization had cleared it, publishing a mute event for a call that had just ended; and — far more seriously — the sequence and timestamp staleness guards were applied to terminal deliveries, so a hangup stamped fractionally behind its predecessor or arriving unsequenced was silently discarded, leaving the session live forever with `CallEnded` never published, wrap-up never started, and the agent and reservation never released. Falsified with 9 probes: reverting the terminal-bypass fix (2 fail), reverting the terminal-mute fix (1), corrupting the production lifecycle rank table (1), removing terminal absorption (1), dropping the recording `EndedUtc` on terminal (1), mapping `Ended` to a live interaction status (1), and stopping the delivery shuffle (1). Three probes initially *failed to falsify* and each exposed a real weakness in the tests rather than in the product, all three fixed before the item was ticked: the rank-table probe was masked by the staleness guards until late regressions were generated; the terminal-absorption probe was invisible until a second competing terminal was generated; and the reordering oracle compared list *lengths*, which injected deliveries always changed, until it was rewritten to compare the first-occurrence subsequence of delivery ids. One probe is recorded as intentionally unfalsifiable in isolation: neutering the service-level idempotency dedup alone changes nothing observable because the publisher deduplicates the same key, and neutering the publisher alone changes nothing because the service already suppressed the redelivery. The two layers are genuinely redundant defense in depth; removing both together falsifies 2 properties, which is recorded here rather than presented as single-layer coverage.

## 11. Gap-closure amendment (2026-07-26)

W0–W9 above were scoped to *ship a credible voice-ACD release*. They were **not** scoped to close every board finding. An audit of all 8 specialist reports against W0–W9 found **47 findings with no owning task, 3 partially covered, and 2 defects in this plan itself** (both now fixed in §2.2: `take-over` was certified by a gate for an unimplemented feature; `recording` was certified by a gate that mono-only recording would pass).

W10–W16 below close the unowned findings. §12 states honestly which review dimensions can and cannot reach a perfect score inside this release.

### W10 — Domain model and code-quality debt
Closes: data F-09, orchard F-05, F-06, F-07, F-12, F-13, telephony 3.1, 1.5, 2.3.

- **W10.1 De-anemize the aggregates.** Every aggregate (`Interaction`, `CallSession`, `ActivityReservation`, `QueueItem`, `AgentSession`, `ContactCenterWorkState`) currently exposes public setters and delegates all rules to services. Convert to private setters plus intention-revealing methods (`Answer`, `Hold`, `Resume`, `Transfer`, `Abandon`, `Complete`). Illegal transitions throw rather than being prevented only by a rank comparison.
  - **Exit:** a test asserts no public setter remains on any aggregate; a state-machine transition table is exhaustively tested including every illegal edge.
- **W10.2 Value objects over primitives.** `PhoneNumber` (E.164-validated, one canonical parser — retires the duplicate normalizers behind data F-06/dist F18), `Duration`, `SkillTag`, and strongly-typed `InteractionId`/`QueueId`/`AgentId`. Kills primitive obsession and the ambiguous-match class of bug at the type level.
- **W10.3 Decompose `VoiceContactCenterCallRouter`** (23 constructor dependencies, 683 LOC) into an ordered, individually testable routing pipeline. 23 dependencies is not a style complaint: it means the class has 23 reasons to change and cannot be unit-tested without 23 fakes.
- **W10.4 Collapse controller duplication.** ~1,700 duplicated LOC across six catalog CRUD controllers → one generic base. Every future catalog entity then inherits authorization, paging, validation, and audit for free.
- **W10.5 `ProviderVoiceEvent` → immutable record.** It is simultaneously a public provider contract and an internally mutated buffer. Make it immutable; mutation via `with`.
- **W10.6 Open the channel model.** `enum InteractionChannel` is closed; the product promises channel extensibility. Replace with a registry-backed channel descriptor. This is a prerequisite for chat/email/SMS in Track B, so doing it now avoids a second breaking change.
- **W10.7 Decompose the two remaining mega-files:** `AsteriskContactCenterVoiceProvider.cs` (2,401 LOC) and `EnterpriseInteractionReportProvider.cs` (1,501 LOC).
- **W10.8 Fix the scoped report factory** that closes over mutable state (orchard F-13) — a latent cross-request data-leak shape.
- **W10.9 Provider-neutral transfer targets and outcomes.** Transfer target types and transfer/merge/snoop outcome metadata still leak Asterisk key names into caller code.

### W11 — Feature graph, public API, and Orchard idiom
Closes: orchard F-01, F-02, F-04, F-08, F-09, F-10, F-14, F-15, F-16.

- **W11.1 Headless/admin split.** `Queues` (and everything above it) transitively drags in `Omnichannel.Managements` UI. Split every capability into `X` (services) and `X.Admin` (UI). A headless/API-only deployment must be provable.
  - **Exit:** a test enables the full headless closure and asserts no admin/UI feature is activated.
- **W11.2 `ContactCenter.Admin` is a manifest-only marker** — enabling it has zero code effect. Either give it the admin registrations (with W11.1) or delete it. A feature that does nothing is a support liability.
- **W11.3 `Analytics` must declare the `Voice`/`Routing` closure its reports actually read**, or degrade explicitly. Today it silently produces wrong reports when enabled alone.
- **W11.4 Feature-dependency audit.** **DONE** (`ContactCenterFeatureDependencyAuditTests`). Add a test that every used service's feature is declared. This is the general fix for the class of bug W0.7 patched pointwise (orchard F-03).
  - **Delivered:** each feature is booted alone in an isolated tenant and every interface in the Contact Center and Telephony assemblies is resolved, individually and as `IEnumerable<T>`. The oracle is *registered but unconstructable*: not registered → `null` → correct (the owning feature is off); registered but throwing → always a manifest defect. No false positives by construction. Plus `EveryFeature_DeclaresDependenciesThatExist` and `NoFeature_DeclaresACircularDependency`.
  - **Found and fixed:** `ICallControlAuthorizationService`, `ISupervisorQueueAuthorizationService` and `ITransferDestinationResolver` were registered in the base feature but depend on Agents/Queues services. Every consumer injected them *optionally* and fail-**open**ed when absent — including keeping a caller-supplied `ProviderCallId` (IDOR on a live call) and skipping outbound-dial ownership (toll fraud). Registrations moved to Voice and Queues; all optional parameters made mandatory; every fail-open branch deleted. Closed permanently by `ContactCenterOptionalDependencyTests`, which rejects *any* optional injected collaborator in either Contact Center assembly.
  - **Also fixed (pre-existing, surfaced by this work):** system-initiated `Reject`/`SendToVoicemail` for closed entry points and unroutable queues carry no agent user and were therefore denied by the agent-ownership boundary, so those calls were never hung up at the provider. Call control now models the initiator (`CallControlInitiator.System`), resolving the provider call id from the server-owned interaction — no call session exists that early — restricted to the `Decline`/`Voicemail` verbs and never granting supervisor privilege.
  - **Rejected as unsound — do not retry:** `ITypeFeatureProvider` is *not* a valid oracle for "what did this feature register". `ExtensionManager` harvests every public non-abstract class in the module assembly into the feature named by a type-level `[Feature]` attribute, falling back to the module-named feature, *before* `ShellContainerFactory.PopulateTypeFeatureProvider` adds DI descriptors with a non-overwriting `TryAdd`. The map is the union of both. Measured: 147 types attributed to a base-only tenant, including types whose startup never ran.
  - **Disclosed limitation — the "every declared dependency is used" half is not enforceable.** `EnableFeaturesAsync` always enables a feature together with its full declared closure, so no tenant can be booted with one dependency removed. Nor is a static oracle sound: `Voice.SoftPhone → RealTime` looks unused by DI (its startup registers no RealTime service) but is genuinely required — `ContactCenterSoftPhoneWidgetDisplayDriver` emits `GetPathByHub<ContactCenterHub>()`, a hub mapped only by RealTime. A gate would have failed on its first run as a false positive and been suppressed. Unused declared dependencies remain a code-review concern.
- **W11.5 Recipes and deployment steps for all Contact Center configuration** (queues, skills, routing profiles, dispositions, business hours, provider connections). Without these, a customer cannot script a tenant, promote dev→prod, or restore config from source control — table stakes for a distributed commercial Orchard module.
- **W11.6 Stream the voice-webhook body.** Reading the full request body into a `string` under a per-request lease is a memory-pressure attack vector on an unauthenticated-ish edge.
- **W11.7 Business rules out of display drivers.** Rules that must hold on *every* write path currently live in a display driver, so API and recipe writes bypass them. One validation path, invoked by driver, controller, and recipe alike.
- **W11.8 Public API surface audit + approval test.** Every public type: should it be public, sealed, immutable, or exist at all? Lock the result with a `PublicApiGenerator` baseline so surface changes become deliberate review events.
- **W11.9 Fix the agent-workspace N+1.**

### W12 — Telephony and media completeness
Closes: telephony 3.1, 3.2, 3.3, 4.5, 4.6, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4, 6.1, 7.2, 7.3, 8.1, 8.2 and the table-stakes gap.

- **W12.1 Dual-channel (stereo) recording — blocking for the `recording` capability.** `AsteriskContactCenterVoiceProvider.cs:459` calls `_ariClient.StartBridgeRecordingAsync(bridgeId, recordingName, AsteriskAriConstants.RecordingFormat, ...)`. Asterisk bridge recording (`POST /bridges/{id}/record`) produces a **single mixed mono file** — there is no per-leg capture anywhere in the tree (a repo-wide search for stereo/dual-channel recording returns zero hits). Every downstream product expectation — agent-vs-customer diarized transcription, talk-over and silence analytics, QM scoring, AI summarization — requires separated legs, and none of them can be retrofitted onto mixed audio. Implement per-leg capture (snoop-per-channel, or `MixMonitor` with the `b` option) and merge to a two-channel artifact. Shipping mono while certifying the `recording` capability would be a false claim of the exact kind RC-3 describes.
- **W12.2 Supervisor take-over is dead surface — the defect was in this plan, not the product.** `MonitorMode.TakeOver` (`MonitorMode.cs:26`), the `TakeOver` capability bit (`ContactCenterVoiceProviderCapabilities.cs:78`) and its entry in `ContactCenterMonitoringService._monitorModes` (`:21`) all exist, but **no provider implements it**: Asterisk deliberately omits `TakeOver` from its declared capabilities (`AsteriskContactCenterVoiceProvider.cs:83-90`), and the mode switch (`:1591-1618`) falls through to `_ => Failure("monitor_mode_unsupported")` at `:1617`. The runtime behaviour is therefore *correct and honest* — the mode is filtered out by capability before it can be invoked. **This is not a production defect and needs no urgent fix.** What was wrong is that §2.2 of this plan previously certified `take-over` for release via `gate-supervision-audio-proof` — a gate that could never pass, for a feature no provider implements. §2.2 is corrected; the capability stays prohibited. Either implement it properly (supervisor joins, agent leg drops, interaction ownership transfers) or delete the enum value, capability bit and mode-list entry so the surface stops advertising an unbuilt feature.
  - **Generalized root cause:** capability bits can exist with no implementation anywhere and nothing detects it. Add `gate-capability-implemented` — every bit in `ContactCenterVoiceProviderCapabilities` must be declared by at least one in-tree provider **and** exercised by at least one test, or be explicitly listed as reserved. This closes the class, not the instance.
- **W12.3 Media security and codec correctness.** Remove the hardcoded `format=ulaw` on external media; enforce SRTP/DTLS at the application layer rather than assuming transport config; enforce TURN credential lifetime alongside the HMAC.
- **W12.4 Explicit call state machine + verified reconciliation.** Legal transitions declared as data, not implied by rank comparison. Prove `ITelephonyCallStateProvider`'s Asterisk implementation actually queries live ARI — reconciliation that reads local state is not reconciliation.
- **W12.5 Idempotency from event identity, not payload hash.** SHA-256 over the raw ARI payload breaks on any upstream serialization change, silently converting duplicate suppression into duplicate processing.
- **W12.6 Orphan sweeper.** Reap orphaned bridges/channels and snoop channels leaked by crash-in-the-middle. Without this, a PBX accumulates zombie resources until manual intervention.
- **W12.7 PBX failover.** Multiple ARI endpoints with health-based selection. A single PBX with no failover makes the PBX a hard SPOF regardless of how many app nodes exist.
- **W12.8 Media quality telemetry** — MOS, jitter, packet loss, one-way delay per call leg. Without these the answer to "why did the call sound bad?" is permanently unavailable.
- **W12.9 Telephony table stakes** absent today: inbound DTMF/IVR digit collection, music-on-hold, call park, and CLI presentation rules (privacy/withheld, per-queue outbound identity).
- **W12.10 STIR/SHAKEN attestation passthrough** for US outbound. Increasingly a carrier-side requirement, not a nice-to-have.
- **W12.11 Replace the magic 1,000-event channel bound** with a documented, load-derived value plus a saturation metric and alert.

### W13 — Omnichannel/CRM layer review
Closes: challenger gap "CRM is an unreviewed production dependency".

The Contact Center depends on Omnichannel/CRM for the universal work item, yet that layer was never reviewed. Run the same review depth over it — authorization boundaries, migration safety, concurrency/CAS, retention, PII handling, background schedulers, tenant isolation — and fold its findings into this plan before release. **Shipping on an unreviewed dependency is how a "hardened" system fails in production.**

### W14 — Product-wide accessibility, localization, and UX
Extends W6 (agent desktop only) to the whole product.

- **W14.1** Admin UI, supervisor dashboard, and report views to WCAG 2.2 AA — the same bar as the agent desktop. Procurement audits the whole product, not one screen.
- **W14.2** Automated a11y gate (axe) across all Contact Center views, not a single page.
- **W14.3** Full localization: no enum `.ToString()` over the wire, no browser-default `toLocaleString()`, localized report headers/exports/notification templates, RTL verified, and a per-tenant/per-user timezone and locale contract (pairs with W9's UTC-only reporting fix).

### W15 — Upgrade, versioning, and deployment safety
Closes: ops F-DEP-01, F-DEP-02, F-DEP-03, F-DEP-04, and the missing N-1 test.

- **W15.1 Event/document upcasters.** `SchemaVersion` exists on persisted documents but nothing reads it. The first schema change after GA is unrecoverable without this.
- **W15.2 Additive-only migration enforcement test** — fail CI on any destructive column/table operation (the existing `UpdateFrom3Async` drop is the precedent). **DONE.** Every Orchard data migration is parsed and checked by three oracles, because each is blind to what the others see: schema-builder operations (`DropColumn`, `DropIndex`, `DropTable`, `RenameColumn`, `RenameTable`, `AlterColumn`), raw SQL passed as an argument to any synchronous or asynchronous execution method, and raw SQL assigned to a command's text — the last being the dominant raw-SQL shape in this repository and one an argument-only oracle would miss entirely. The raw-SQL oracles deliberately do not scan string literals: ordinary C# defeats that, since `"drop " + "table " + name` and `$"drop {kind} {name}"` are both destructive and neither contains a matching literal. The statement is reconstructed from the syntax tree across concatenation, interpolation, single-assignment locals, and read-only query-builder composition, then classified, so it is judged on what it does rather than on how it was spelled; a builder composed with any operation outside the read-only set falls back to unreadable rather than being assumed safe, and because that read-only special case is only sound while the single `SqlBuilder` in scope is the data layer's, a separate fact fails if the repository ever declares **or aliases** a type by that name, since `using SqlBuilder = Something;` is the same impersonation without the declaration. Classification does not stop at the leading verb: `with doomed as (...) delete from t` leads with `with`, and a batch can hide a second statement after a semicolon, so a destructive verb anywhere in the statement is a finding. Quoted values are stripped before that scan so a value that merely reads like a verb is not a false positive, and a statement that can execute another statement (`exec`, `sp_executesql`, or a procedural `do`/`begin` block, wherever it appears) is classified as unreadable rather than safe, since the gate can see the wrapper but not what it runs — without this, stripping quoted values would clear `DO $$ BEGIN EXECUTE 'DROP TABLE t'; END $$;`. A statement the gate cannot read is itself a finding, recorded per call site with what it does and why it cannot be destructive, because otherwise `ExecuteAsync(statement)` would be a one-line bypass. Such an approval is pinned to a fingerprint of the **declaring type**, not the call site: the approved expression here calls a sibling helper, so pinning the expression alone would let a change to what that helper builds inherit the old approval. Attribution is syntactic, so a destructive step is bound to the private helper that performs it rather than to the step that calls it — exactly the cases a line-proximity heuristic would mis-attribute. Each destructive step needs a register entry authorizing **one operation against one named object**, and an entry that matches no step or several steps fails: registering a method instead would make every entry a standing bypass of whatever that method later does. Justifications are machine-checked, not prose. A contract-phase entry must name a strictly older release as the one that introduced the object, which mechanically prevents expand and contract landing in the same release. A never-released entry must additionally name the **database object** it is about, and that claim is checked by searching the source of every stable release tag for it. The version alone is an author's assertion the gate cannot check — an object that shipped in `1.2.2` could be declared as introduced in `2.0.0` and the version rule would still clear it, because no stable `2.0.0` tag exists. Naming the introducing commit only relocates the assertion, since any recent untagged commit satisfies it; searching the released source checks the claim itself. The claim also has to be bound to the object the entry actually operates on. A schema operation names its object directly, so the claim must equal it. Raw SQL is read at the operand position — the identifier following `drop table`, `alter table`, `delete from`, and the like — rather than anywhere in the statement, because matching the object anywhere accepts it appearing in a trailing comment while a different table is dropped. Reconstruction is what makes that position readable, resolving constants, interpolation holes, table quoting, schema qualification, and index-table naming conventions; the interpolation case in particular required recursing into the holes, without which `$"drop table {quotedTable}"` reconstructed to `drop table ?`. Every operand in the statement must be the claimed object rather than only the first, so a batch that drops the authorized table and then a second, unauthorized one is rejected instead of being covered by one claim, and an operand that cannot be read is a finding rather than a pass. Without that binding, changing the constant that names the dropped table would leave the statement classification, the authorization, and the claim all unchanged while dropping something else entirely. Stable tags stop at `v1.2.2`, and none of the eight registered objects appears in that tree. The check fails closed when the released source cannot be read or no stable tags exist, since treating "no tags" as "nothing released" would turn the strongest rule into the weakest; CI therefore checks out with `fetch-depth: 0`. Prerelease tags are excluded deliberately: upgrading from a preview or RC is not a supported path, and that is a stated boundary rather than an oversight. `UninstallAsync` is exempt, and only `UninstallAsync`, because uninstall is not an upgrade path. Because the gate finds migrations by folder convention while Orchard finds them by registration, that convention is verified: every type passed to `AddDataMigration` must appear in the scanned surface. Scope boundary: destructive DDL executed from a background task, recipe, feature event handler, or service is outside this gate and is disclosed as such in the production-support documentation.
- **W15.3 N-1 rolling-upgrade test:** old and new schema/code versions running against one database, both healthy. This is what makes the zero-downtime claim in the deployment docs true rather than aspirational.
- **W15.4 Canary + rollback runbook**, exercised in CI, not just described.
- **W15.5 Telephony command handler must drain on shutdown**, not cancel — cancelling in-flight commands mid-call during a deploy drops live calls.

### W16 — Residual distributed and data hygiene
Closes: dist F14, F15, F16, F18, F19, F22; data F-08, F-10, F-11, F-13, F-14, F-15, F-16; plus the Elasticsearch verification.

- **W16.1** Run call-teardown services only on terminal events (currently every event runs all of them).
- **W16.2** Hub group-join sequences must not use `Context.ConnectionAborted` — partial group membership on a flaky client silently drops that agent's events. Establish and test one hub cancellation convention.
- **W16.3** Readiness gate before the ARI listener starts on shell activation.
- **W16.4** `ContactCenterEventMetric` daily counter: replace the hot-row read-modify-write with an append-and-rollup (or atomic increment). At tier-1 rates this row is a serialization point.
- **W16.5** `AgentSession` heartbeat must not be a full-document CAS write; bound `ListAsync` calls; make the retention cutoff scan index-seekable.
- **W16.6** Reduce sequential store round-trips inside the reservation lock; add lease renewal for long operations.
- **W16.7** Column sizing correction (`nvarchar(261)`, `nvarchar(128)`).
- **W16.8** Add a test proving no Contact Center correctness path depends on Elasticsearch (the support matrix asserts this; nothing enforces it). **DONE.** A search dependency can arrive through three independent mechanisms, and an oracle covering one is blind to the others. A CLR reference is the compile-time mechanism: the transitive reference closure of every shipped Contact Center, Telephony, Asterisk, and DialPad assembly is walked and any Elasticsearch or OpenSearch client reached at any depth fails the build, and direct references are additionally checked against a wider list covering Lucene and the Orchard search and indexing abstractions. An Orchard feature dependency is the runtime mechanism and is a *string* in a manifest with no CLR reference at all, so an assembly-only gate would stay green while a feature pulled an entire search module into every tenant that enabled it; a manifest gate and a real-tenant enabled-feature-closure gate cover it. The closure is read with `MetadataReader` rather than `Assembly.Load`, because loading forces every transitive dependency to resolve and swallowing a load failure would let a violation hide behind an intermediate assembly, and traversal completeness is asserted rather than assumed. The direct half is deliberately not transitive: measurement showed the closure legitimately reaches an embedded Lucene index through shared libraries depended on for unrelated reasons, and an in-process index needs no cluster and no operator action, so banning it transitively would report a dependency the module does not have and would turn the gate into something engineers suppress. Measurement also proved `OrchardCore.Indexing` is enabled by the platform baseline rather than by any Contact Center feature, so the enabled-feature gate targets search *engines* and reports the cause of every enabled feature it rejects. A further fact pins the directory-driven assembly discovery to an exact set, so the gate cannot pass vacuously by finding nothing. Static analysis alone cannot see a correctness path that reaches a cluster through an ordinary HTTP client, so a runtime fact executes routing selection, assignment through a real reservation, outbox dispatch, and provider ingest through the normalized voice-event seam every PBX adapter funnels into (including its replay suppression) against persisted state inside a real supported-profile tenant, with every outbound HTTP request in the process recorded and required to be empty; the recorder proves it is attached by observing a self-test request rather than assuming attachment. Executing those paths immediately found a pre-existing defect that made every successful outbox dispatch throw, which the existing mock-session tests could not reproduce; it is fixed and pinned against a real store. What remains unproved is behaviour with the search binaries physically absent, which needs a packaging harness and is disclosed as a follow-up rather than claimed.

- **W16.9** Decide the fate of the generic provider webhook ingress. Executing W16.8's runtime fact found that `IProviderVoiceWebhookAdapter` has **no concrete implementation anywhere in the product**: only the contract, the abstract `HmacProviderVoiceWebhookAdapterBase`, and `ProviderVoiceWebhookProcessor` ship, and every implementor is a test fake. `ProcessAsync` therefore returns `UnknownProvider` for every request in every supported profile. Both shipping PBX integrations ingest through the normalized `IProviderVoiceEventService` seam instead. Either an adapter is a missing provider integration and must be built and gated, or the generic webhook ingress is unused surface that falls under the legacy-and-cleanup mandate and must be removed rather than left as an HMAC-verified endpoint no request can ever satisfy. Shipping an authenticated public ingress with no implementation behind it is the worse of the two outcomes, so this must be resolved before GA rather than deferred.

## 12. What a re-review can and cannot score 10/10

This section exists because the honest answer to "will this make everything 10/10?" is **partly**.

| Dimension | After W0–W9 | After W0–W16 (Track A) | Ceiling cause |
|---|---|---|---|
| Architecture | 7.5 | **9.0** | Residual: the domain model is being retrofitted, not designed from scratch. |
| Code Quality | 8.0 | **9.0** | — |
| Security | 7.5 | **9.0** | Requires an external penetration test, and erasure (W17) proven end-to-end, to go higher. |
| Reliability | 7.0 | **8.5** | Single PBX and single app node cap blast-radius containment; the W1 cutover carries residual risk until shadow replay is clean. |
| Testing | 8.0 | **9.0** | 10 requires sustained mutation-score and chaos evidence over time, not a one-off gate. |
| Documentation | 8.5 | **9.5** | 10 requires rehearsed drills behind every operational claim, not prose. |
| Operational Readiness | 7.5 | **9.0** | 10 requires production telemetry from real customers. |
| **Scalability** | 5.0 | **6.5** | **Structurally capped — see below.** |
| **Contact Center Domain** | 6.5 | **7.0** | **Structurally capped — see below.** |

> **Scores revised down 2026-07-26** after the independent challenge graded the original table's honesty **4/10**. The original claimed "7 dimensions reach 9.5–10". That was aspirational: it assumed every gate would be both implemented *and* falsifiable, while ~20 ledger entries still had blank gate values and several exit criteria were unmeasurable (§14 findings 4 and 5). Security and Reliability in particular cannot be near-perfect while subject erasure is a dead code path (W17) and the W1 cutover is unproven. **No dimension is claimed at 10.** These numbers are a target to be *earned* by passing gates, not a forecast.

**Scalability cannot reach 10/10 in this release, by construction.** The release topology is one application node. A reviewer asking "does this work at 100,000 users?" gets the answer "this is certified for 100 agents on one node." No amount of code quality changes that. Reaching 10 requires Track B.

**Contact Center Domain cannot reach 10/10 either.** §3 defers skill proficiency and bullseye relaxation, per-channel capacity, virtual hold, chat/email/SMS ingress, predictive dialing, WFM, and QM. Against Genesys/NICE/Five9/Amazon Connect, a voice-only ACD without those is a competent v1, not a 10.

**The choice is explicit:**
- **Track A (W0–W16)** — ship a genuinely production-ready single-node voice contact center. Seven of nine dimensions reach 9.5–10. Two are honestly capped. This is achievable and defensible.
- **Track B** — required to lift the remaining two. Do not start it before Track A completes; it multiplies surface area over an unhardened base, which is exactly the mistake that produced RC-1.

### Track B (post-Track-A, to lift the capped dimensions)

- **B1 — Multi-node certification.** The W3 work makes correctness *possible* on multiple nodes; B1 *proves* it: real multi-process, multi-container tests with induced partitions, Redis failover, and node kills. Flips the support matrix to multi-node production.
- **B2 — Partitioned routing engine.** Replace the per-queue lease with partitioned/sharded assignment so routing throughput scales with node count instead of being serialized per queue. Prerequisite for the 1,000+ agent tier.
- **B3 — Channel completeness.** Chat, email, and SMS ingress on the W10.6 open channel model, with per-channel agent capacity and per-channel presence.
- **B4 — Routing sophistication.** Skill proficiency levels, bullseye/progressive relaxation, service-level-driven and predictive routing.
- **B5 — Domain gap table closure.** Virtual hold, EWT and position announcements, max queue depth and overflow, per-outcome retry scheduling, local presence, list recycling, campaign quotas, occupancy/adherence/FCR.
- **B6 — WFM and QM** — forecasting, scheduling, adherence; scorecards, evaluations, screen recording.
- **B7 — Predictive dialing** with a real in-tree abandonment statistics provider and safe-harbor playback.
- **B8 — Multi-region and data residency enforcement.**
