## 13. Amendment progress ledger (W10–W16)

Same rule as §10: a box is ticked only when its named gate passes in CI.

- [x] W10.1 Aggregates de-anemized; illegal transitions rejected `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test` — `AggregateLifecycleTableTests` (7), `AggregateStateTransitionTests` (17), `AggregateLifecycleArchitectureTests` (5), plus the existing `CallStateMachinePropertyTests` and the full 3,17x-case unit suite exercising every converted call site. **The written gate annotation was `gate:gate-domain-invariants`, which does not exist in the catalog; the row is bound to `pr_ci.yml#build_test` and the new evidence is registered as control-matrix gate `D018`.** All five status-carrying aggregates (`Interaction`, `CallSession`, `QueueItem`, `ActivityReservation`, `ContactCenterWorkState`) were plain property bags: every status was publicly settable, so *can this call move from planned to held* was answered independently by the ingestion service, the command executors, the healing service and the router, and nothing required those answers to agree. **The only ordering rule that existed could not see the defect.** `VoiceStreamOrdering` groups call states into five lifecycle phases, so it can tell whether a change moves the call forward but not whether the edge exists: planned-to-held is forward, so it was admitted, and the record then said the call was on hold without ever having been answered. Every talk time, hold time and wallboard figure computed from it reported the fiction as real, and nothing raised an error, because from each writer's point of view it had set a property. Each status now has a private setter with `[JsonInclude]` and a `TransitionTo` that consults one declared edge table per aggregate; a move no edge admits throws `InvalidStateTransitionException` carrying the aggregate, the status it is in and the status it was asked to reach. Settled statuses have no outgoing edge. Re-applying a held status is admitted so at-least-once redelivery is not turned into an error. `Requeue` and `Reoffer` replace the open-coded status writes at the re-offer sites; both move along declared backwards edges rather than around the table, so both are refused once the session has settled for the same reason everything else is. **Three paths deliberately report rather than decide and are named for it.** `CallSession.MirrorProviderState` and `Interaction.MirrorSessionStatus` (two of the three) exist because the provider owns what a call is doing and ordering for that stream is already enforced upstream — an earlier attempt to *refuse* provider edges here was caught within one test run by `CallStateMachinePropertyTests`, which found the session reporting `Transferred` while the interaction it projects onto had been held at `Created`; re-deciding an already-decided question made the two records disagree, which is worse than the fiction it was trying to prevent. `ContactCenterWorkState.AdoptActivityAssignmentStatus` exists because seeding a work state from an activity that already carries a routing status has no previous status to move from. **Two edges the real services perform were missing from the first draft of the tables and were found by running the suite, not by inspection**: an interaction may become `Transferring` from `Created` and `Ringing`, because a queued item that was never offered can still be moved to another queue, and a call session may reach `Ended` from any alerting state, because providers do not all distinguish why an unanswered call stopped and refusing a plain hangup would strand the session alerting forever with the offer never released. Both are recorded in the tables with the reason. The gate is structural as well as behavioural: the complete N x N matrix of all five lifecycles is compared to a transliteration of each table written in a different shape, which is **a drift alarm, not a proof of correctness** — it catches an edge changed in one place and not the other, but an edge wrong in both would satisfy it, so the claims that matter are asserted separately from the enums and the settled predicates rather than from the edge lists: no settled interaction status and no terminal call state has an outgoing edge, every unsettled interaction status can still reach an ending so nothing is stranded alive, and a planned call is refused the established and unanswered outcomes that imply it was answered; reflection asserts no guarded status has a public setter; every aggregate is round-tripped through `System.Text.Json` because a private setter without `[JsonInclude]` is dropped silently and every persisted aggregate would come back holding the enum default, which reads as a created interaction, a planned call and a waiting queue item; and a scan refuses the test-only restore seam to production code and fails closed if a guarded root or a named file disappears. Falsified with 17 probes across two rounds, 17 detected: reopening the `Interaction.Status` setter, dropping `[JsonInclude]`, widening the call-session table with planned-to-held, giving `Completed` a way back to `Waiting` (3 fail), giving `Rejected` a way to `Accepted` (3 fail), making `CanTransition` return true unconditionally (5 fail), removing the settled guard from `Requeue`, calling the restore seam from `ActivityReservationService`, silently narrowing the guarded roots, dropping the settled guard from the expiry sweep (2 fail), removing both mirror resurrection guards (3 fail), giving `Ended` a call-session edge back to `Connected`, re-admitting planned-to-held against the named refusal, removing the connected-to-ringing re-offer edge (2 fail), stranding `Transferring` with no ending, adding a fifth bypass call site, and dropping the terminal guards from the failure projections (3 fail). **Review found three defects that the tests as first written did not reach, all fixed and gated here.** (1) Refusing to requeue a settled interaction is right, but the expiry sweep releases every due reservation in the tenant from a background task whose per-queue `try`/`catch` does not cover the sweep call, so the ordinary race of a customer hanging up while an offer rings would have abandoned every later reservation in the batch and done so again every tick; the release path now skips the requeue on a settled record and completes the rest of the release. (2) The failure projections in the answer, dial and call-action executors are what let a compensating command finish, so a refusal there would have left the command `Compensating` forever with the exception swallowed by the dispatcher's catch; they now tolerate an already-settled record. (3) Queue transfer was broken outright: the interaction has to reach alerting again from every live status and the call session has to alert again while connected or held, and neither edge was declared, so every queue transfer whose target agent accepted would have thrown. **Mirroring was also tightened**: it now refuses to reopen a settled record, because a record can settle on a path the provider stream never sees, and a structural test pins the two files and four call sites allowed to use the three bypasses so the exception cannot spread. **Deviations recorded honestly rather than faked.** `AgentSession` was surveyed and left unchanged: it records connections and heartbeats and carries no status enum, so there is no lifecycle to declare and inventing one would add ceremony without a rule. The intention-revealing method set is narrower than the item's illustrative list (`Answer`/`Hold`/`Resume`/`Transfer`/`Abandon`/`Complete`): only the operations that were genuinely being open-coded at more than one call site with more than one meaning were introduced, because a method that wraps a single `TransitionTo` used once adds a name without adding an invariant. Only the *status* setters were closed; the remaining properties on these aggregates are still publicly settable, so this constrains what a status may become, not who may write the rest of the record. Strongly-typed `InteractionId`/`QueueId`/`AgentId`, deferred here from W10.2, were **not** delivered: they are YesSql document properties and index columns across the whole module set, so the change is a schema-and-migration exercise whose safety story is the one W2.5 built, and it remains open.
- [x] W10.2 Value objects replace primitives; one canonical E.164 parser `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test` — `PhoneNumberTests` (20 cases), `PhoneNumberCanonicalizationArchitectureTests` (4), `ExternalDestinationPolicyTests` (23), `SkillTagTests` (17), plus the behavioural cases added to `DialerEligibilityServiceTests`, `DialerAttemptServiceTests` and `OmnichannelContactImportRowFilterTests`. **The written gate annotation was `gate:gate-domain-invariants`, which does not exist in the catalog; the row is bound to `pr_ci.yml#build_test` and the new evidence is registered as control-matrix gate `D017`.** There was one parser (`IPhoneNumberService.TryFormatToE164`) and five different answers to what happened when it failed. Four callers stripped the number to its digits, one kept the raw text, and `LocalDncRegistry` dropped it. **That divergence was a live compliance bypass, not a tidiness problem.** `DefaultDialerEligibilityService.Normalize` parsed with no region, so a destination written the way a person writes it failed and became digits; those digits went to `INationalDoNotCallRegistry.GetRegisteredNumbersAsync`; `LocalDncRegistry` re-normalized, failed the same way, dropped the number, queried nothing and returned an empty set; the dialer read that as "not listed" and placed the call. The same fallback also made `GetRegionCode` return null, so the regional calling calendar was silently replaced by the default one. Nothing logged an error, because no component believed anything had gone wrong. `PhoneNumber` is now in E.164 form by construction with no public constructor, so a caller cannot assert canonicality without proving it; `IPhoneNumberService.TryParse` is the one entry point that produces it; the registry contract takes and returns it (**breaking change for custom registries**); the destination is canonicalized once at the top of the evaluation using a new `DialerProfile.DefaultRegionCode`; and a destination that cannot be canonicalized suppresses the attempt rather than being repaired into something no registry can compare. `CanadaDnclRegistry` and `UsaFtcDncRegistry` now skip a number outside their numbering plan instead of stripping its country code and asking about a different number. `PhoneNumberCanonicalizationArchitectureTests` scans the Contact Center, Telephony, do-not-call and Omnichannel management projects for a second parser or hand-rolled normalization, and **fails rather than scanning nothing** when a root it claims to cover no longer exists. **Review caught that the guard originally named the calling and compliance path but excluded the contact-import module, where three of the five original fallbacks still stood verbatim** — including the one that kept the raw text — so the structural defence did not cover half of what the changelog said it did. All three were converted, the module is now guarded, and the looser matching the import genuinely needs (a contact typed in years ago may never have been canonical) is `PhoneNumberComparisonKey`, which is named for comparing rather than identifying so it cannot be mistaken for canonicalization the way its inline predecessors were. `DialerEligibilityServiceTests` was switched from a stub that answered `+15551112222` to every question to the real libphonenumber-backed service, because a stub that always succeeds cannot tell whether the dialer canonicalized anything. **Three adjacent defects were found while proving this one and are fixed and gated with it.** (1) The national registries logged a failed lookup and returned an empty set, so an unreachable or misconfigured registry was indistinguishable from one reporting the number as unlisted — a fail-open compliance check in both the dialer and the contact import. They now raise `DoNotCallScreeningException`; the dialer suppresses with the new `ComplianceScreeningUnavailable` reason, which is deliberately **not** terminal because the destination was never shown to be off limits, only unverified, so the activity is neither dialed nor discarded; the import skips the row with the reason stated. A registry with no credentials is treated as not participating and suppresses nothing. (2) The external-destination dialing rule existed as three identical copies — settings editor, transfer resolver, dial executor — free to drift into a destination the settings screen refuses but a workflow can still reach; consolidated into `ExternalDestinationPolicy`, which carries the original bounds unchanged (at least eight characters of E.164, so seven digits, and at most fifteen digits) and is strictly stricter in only two respects, both a consequence of routing through the value object: a number whose country code begins with zero, and a number written in non-ASCII digits, were accepted by all three copies and are now refused. Nothing that was refused is now allowed. (3) A queue's required skills were trimmed by its editor while an agent's skills, which arrive through recipes, deployments and imports, were not, so an agent whose skill was stored as `" Spanish"` was silently ineligible for every queue requiring `"Spanish"`; both sides now read through `SkillTag`. Falsified with 18 probes, 18 detected: restoring the digits-only fallback (2 fail), sending the raw destination to the registry, ignoring the configured region, loosening the value object to accept a formatted number (3 fail), reaching past the canonical entry point in a guarded file, making skill comparison case-sensitive (5 fail), dropping the skill trim (6 fail), reading the agent side some other way, swallowing a screening failure in the dialer (2 fail), swallowing it in the import, and making the screening failure terminal (2 fail). Seven further probes were run against the strengthening that review prompted, all seven detected: reintroducing digit-stripping in the import row filter, reintroducing a second parser in the duplicate lookup, restoring the drop-on-reparse in the local registry (4 fail), making the JSON converter silently accept a stored value that is not canonical (3 fail), dropping the property-name overrides so a number cannot key a document (2 fail), making the comparison key keep the raw text rather than the digits (5 fail), and quietly narrowing the guarded roots to exclude the import module. **Two further real defects were found by review and fixed rather than documented around.** The local registry reported the *stored* string re-parsed instead of the number the caller asked about, so a stored value the query still matched but the parser no longer accepted was dropped — and a dropped match reads to the dialer as "not listed"; on a provider whose `IN` comparison ignores trailing blanks that is a live fail-open, and it is now resolved back to the queried number and gated by `LocalDncRegistryMatchResolutionTests`. And `PhoneNumberJsonConverter` rejected a bad stored value with an `ArgumentException`, which escapes the serializer without the property path that says which document is wrong, and had no property-name overrides, so keying anything by a number would have thrown at runtime for the first feature that tried it. **Deviations recorded honestly rather than faked.** `Duration` was not introduced: every duration in the domain is already named with its unit at the point of use (`SlaThresholdSeconds`, `RetryDelayMinutes`, `AbandonmentRollingWindowMinutes`), so the ambiguity the item targets does not exist there, and wrapping them would churn persisted models for no invariant. Strongly-typed `InteractionId`/`QueueId`/`AgentId` were not introduced: they appear in YesSql document properties and index columns across the whole module set, so the change is a schema-and-migration exercise rather than a typing one, and it is deferred to be done with W10.1's aggregate work where the same documents are already being rewritten. Persisted skill and phone collections remain `IList<string>` with normalization applied at every boundary, for the same migration-safety reason; the invariant is enforced where values are compared, not by rewriting stored documents. `IContactCenterSkillStore.FindByNameAsync` remains case-sensitive and is left alone because it has no callers.

- [x] W10.5 `ProviderVoiceEvent` immutable `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test` — `ProviderVoiceEventImmutabilityTests` (10 executed cases); full suite 3,057 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped. The type was a public provider contract that ingestion also mutated: it canonicalized the provider identity onto the caller's own instance and rewrote the idempotency key in place, so ingestion defended itself with a hand-written `CloneProviderEvent`. That copy was a separate thing to keep complete and it was not — it dropped `HangupCause`, and because a session infers a cause when none is supplied, every call reported the inferred cause rather than the provider's, with nothing anywhere to say the real one had been lost. It is now a `sealed record` whose every property is init-only; ingestion derives its adjusted event with `with`, which copies every member by construction, and the clone and the test that policed its completeness are both gone. `Metadata` is exposed as `IReadOnlyDictionary<string, string>` and snapshotted on assignment, preserving the comparer the provider supplied, so a caller holding its own reference to the dictionary cannot change an event it has already handed over. Two call sites that mutated after construction were rewritten rather than papered over: the webhook processor's `ProviderName ??=` default now derives the event from the parsed one, and the ingestion retry re-derives its adjustments from the event as handed in rather than replaying a mutated copy. **The written gate annotation was `gate:gate-public-api-approved`, which belongs to W11.8 and does not exist yet; the row is therefore bound to `pr_ci.yml#build_test`, and W11.8 will subsume it.** **Review found two real weaknesses and both were fixed rather than documented around.** (1) The snapshot recovered the comparer only from a `Dictionary<string, string>`; every other implementation fell through to ordinal comparison silently — including the type the property itself returns, so the documented way to adjust an event (deriving it from one you already hold) downgraded a provider's case-insensitive metadata to case-sensitive on every derivation, which is the same "plausible substitute with nothing to say the real value was lost" failure this item exists to end. The snapshot now passes its own type through unchanged and recovers the comparer from `Dictionary`, `ConcurrentDictionary`, `ImmutableDictionary` and `FrozenDictionary`; a source that cannot report one is keyed ordinally, which is the only honest choice when the source will not say how it compares its own keys. (2) The aliasing half of the gate was written against `Metadata` by name while the structural half accepted `IReadOnlyList<>`/`IReadOnlyCollection<>`/`IEnumerable<>` as proof of immutability — but a read-only *interface* guarantees nothing about aliasing, so an init-only `IReadOnlyList<string>` assigned a caller-owned `List<string>` would have passed every case while leaving the event mutable through the caller's reference. That was a real reduction in strength against the completeness test it replaced, which was structural over every declared property by construction. The sweep is now structural too: for every collection property it builds a mutable instance, assigns it, grows the caller's copy and fails if the event changed with it, and a reference-typed property whose shape it cannot build is reported rather than skipped, because skipping is how a sweep like this quietly stops covering the member that needed it most. Falsified with 8 probes, 8 detected: making one property settable, aliasing the caller's metadata dictionary instead of snapshotting it, typing `Metadata` as a mutable `IDictionary<,>`, losing the record-ness (caught by the clone-method assertion), dropping the non-`Dictionary` comparer arms (1), additionally dropping the snapshot pass-through so derivation loses the comparer (2 fail), adding an init-only `IReadOnlyList<string>` aliased from the caller (1), and adding a reference-typed property the sweep cannot sample (2 fail).

- [x] W11.1 Headless/admin feature split `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test, contact_center_feature_activation_matrix.yml#fresh-tenant-activation` — `ContactCenterHeadlessClosureTests` (3 executed tests) plus the regenerated feature-graph ledger; full suite 3,211 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped, activation suite 44 passed / 2 skipped, distributed suite 16 passed / 1 failed (the pre-existing Redis-backplane case, no broker available). **The written gate annotation was `gate:gate-headless-closure`, which does not exist in the catalog; the row is bound to `pr_ci.yml#build_test` and the new evidence is registered as control-matrix gate `F008`.** The item as written described `Queues` transitively dragging `Omnichannel.Managements` in, but the coupling was broader than one edge: **every** capability feature registered its own admin menus and display drivers, and the base feature itself depended on the management module, so a headless tenant received the entire CRM administration experience the moment it enabled anything at all. Each capability now registers services only, and the screens it used to register live in a matching `.Admin` feature that depends on the capability rather than the other way round — the direction is what makes the guarantee hold, because a capability can no longer name a UI feature at all. The split had to cross module boundaries to mean anything: `Omnichannel.Managements` is now the administration experience layered over a new headless `CrestApps.OrchardCore.Omnichannel.Activities` feature that owns the catalogs, stores, content parts, indexes, migrations, permissions and subject-disposition endpoint, and the Telephony settings screen moved to a new `CrestApps.OrchardCore.Telephony.Admin`; a capability that transitively drags an administration module in is no more headless than one that registers the screens itself. **The oracle is structural, not a list of feature names.** The test boots one tenant with the whole headless closure, then discovers by reflection every `INavigationProvider` and every closed `IDisplayDriver<>` implementation in the Contact Center, Telephony and Omnichannel assemblies and asserts the tenant resolves none of them — so a screen added to a capability feature later fails without anyone remembering to extend the test. That oracle found five leftovers the manifest reading had missed: the base feature still registered `ContactCenterExternalTransferSettingsDisplayDriver` and `ContactCenterSettingsAdminMenu`, `Recording` still registered `ContactCenterRecordingSettingsDisplayDriver`, and Telephony still registered its settings driver and admin menu. **It also found a defect that no manifest or dependency test could have found:** the six new admin startup classes had been placed inside another class, and Orchard's extension harvester does not see nested types, so they compiled, were attributed with `[Feature]`, and never ran. The exclusion list cannot be used to weaken the closure, because `EveryUserExperienceFeature_ActuallyServesAUserInterface` boots each excluded feature alone and requires it to register Contact Center or Telephony surface of its own — restricted to those assemblies precisely because surface inherited through a declared dependency would otherwise make the requirement vacuous. Falsified with 6 probes, 6 detected: putting an admin menu back on a capability feature, putting a display driver back on one, pointing the base feature at `Omnichannel.Managements` again, adding a headless feature to the user-experience exclusion list, emptying an administration startup, and nesting a startup class inside another type. **Probe 3 initially passed, which was itself the finding:** a per-iteration diagnostic string left in the administration oracle made its `Except(...)` set-difference trivially non-empty and had silently disabled the test; the diagnostic was removed and the probe then bit. **Review found a second, worse half of the same defect and it is fixed rather than documented around.** Moving the display drivers to `.Admin` while leaving the seven catalog controllers attributed to their capability was not a smaller version of the leak - it was a data-integrity bug. Orchard gates controllers by `[Feature]`, so on a capability-only tenant the `/Admin/contact-center/queues`, `skills`, `queue-groups`, `business-hours`, `agent-state-reason-codes`, `dialer-profiles` and `entry-points` routes stayed registered and still authorized, while the drivers that are the only model-binding and validation path for them no longer resolved: `UpdateEditorAsync` bound nothing, `ModelState.IsValid` was trivially true, and the create post persisted a nameless, group-less catalog record that the headless routing stack then consumed. **That state was every upgraded tenant**, because this change deliberately ships no upgrade migration. The nine `[Admin]` controllers were re-attributed to the feature that owns their screens - `AgentSoftPhoneController` to `VoiceSoftPhone`, whose widget views post to it and whose closure already contains the presence manager it needs - and the oracle was extended to enumerate routed `[Admin]` controllers from the tenant's own `IActionDescriptorCollectionProvider`, so the sweep now covers routes and not only services. Probe: returning `QueuesController` to the `Queues` feature fails the headless closure. **Review also found the exclusion-list guard asymmetric with the administration guard, and it is fixed.** Test 2 required only that an excluded feature resolve some Contact Center surface, without subtracting what it inherits - and because all six `.Admin` features depend on the administration root, every one of them satisfied it on the root's screens alone, whatever it registered itself. Both guards now measure a feature's *own* contribution: the feature's declared dependency closure is booted with the feature withheld, that surface is the baseline, and the feature must add Contact Center or Telephony surface beyond it. Probe: emptying an administration startup now fails both guards, where before the fix it failed only the administration one. The reviewer's related concern - that padding the exclusion list with a capability could hide a regression - was tested rather than assumed and does not hold: adding `Queues` to the list fails the closure anyway, because headless features depend on it and it is therefore still enabled transitively, which the same test asserts against. **Deviations recorded rather than faked.** `VoiceSoftPhone`, `AgentDesktop`, `Supervision`, `Analytics` and `Maintenance` were not split: they exist to serve a user interface and nothing would remain behind, and each is listed in the test's exclusion set and required to prove it serves one. No automatic upgrade migration enables the new `.Admin` features: the in-repo pattern for that (`ShellSettings.IsInitializing()` plus a deferred `EnableFeaturesAsync`) races any other shell-descriptor mutation in the same request and threw `Invalid serial number for shell descriptor` on two previously-passing activation tests, so the module set being unreleased, the upgrade is documented as a manual step in the changelog and the Contact Center overview instead of shipped as a mechanism that can fail at tenant start.

Deleting it was rejected in favour of making it real because the five new capability administration features need one place to own the shared menu, and duplicating that registration five times would reintroduce exactly the drift this item exists to end. **A marker feature that does nothing cannot come back**, because the gate boots each administration feature alone and requires it to resolve navigation providers or display drivers beyond those it inherits from the administration root — the subtraction is what makes the requirement real, since every one of them depends on the root and would otherwise pass on the root's screens alone. - [x] W11.3 `Analytics` declares its capability closure `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test, contact_center_feature_activation_matrix.yml#fresh-tenant-activation` — `ContactCenterReportCapabilityDegradationTests` (4 executed tests) and `ContactCenterReportDataProvenanceArchitectureTests` (1 executed test), registered as control-matrix gate `F009`; full suite 3,212 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped, activation suite 47 passed / 2 skipped, distributed suite 16 passed / 1 failed (the pre-existing Redis-backplane case, no broker available), docs build succeeded. **The written gate annotation was `gate:gate-feature-dependency-audit`, a static manifest audit that cannot prove a runtime degradation; the row is bound to the jobs that run the two new proofs and the deviation is recorded here.** **The item's premise was investigated rather than implemented, and it was half wrong in one direction and badly incomplete in the other.** Walking every persisted field the reports read back to the code that writes it showed `Routing` is not a data producer for these reports at all — queue wait, ASA and abandonment are derived in the report from interaction timestamps — while `Voice` and `Recording` are: `Interaction.ProviderName` is written only by the voice call-state and routing services, `Interaction.TransferHistory` only by the voice transfer service, and `Interaction.RecordingReference` only by the recording service. **The same walk found two reports measuring fields that nothing in the product has ever written.** `CallLegPerformance` read `Interaction.CallLegs`, a property declared on the interaction and assigned by no code path anywhere — legs have been projected onto `CallSession.Legs` by `CallTopologyProjector` since W2.2 — so it rendered an empty table on every tenant, enabled capabilities or not. `TranscriptCoverage` read `Interaction.TranscriptReference`, likewise never written, and published a confident 0% coverage on every tenant; transcripts are a future quality-management pillar in `PLAN.md`, not an implemented capability. Neither is a reporting bug that a capability declaration would have fixed: they are reports about data that does not exist. `CallLegPerformance` was rewired to read the call session the projector maintains, `TranscriptCoverage` was withdrawn, and both dead members plus the `InteractionCallLeg` type were deleted. **The plan's `or degrade explicitly` branch was taken deliberately, and the alternative is worse.** Adding `Voice` and `Recording` to the `Analytics` manifest would make a tenant that runs chat and CRM only enable, secure and upgrade voice call handling in order to read a queue report — precisely the coupling W11.1 removed, reintroduced one layer up. Analytics therefore declares neither, and the affected reports return a notice naming the missing feature instead of a document of zeroes. The distinction is not cosmetic: zero is a measurement, an absent capability took none, and `recording coverage: 0%` read by a compliance officer on a tenant that never had recording is a false operational statement. **The declaration is required of every Contact Center report, not only the ones that need it**, so a report cannot be added without deciding what produces its data; because the enterprise and workforce reports are one provider class each parameterized by ~50 registrations, the requirement rides on the report *kind* rather than the registration call, which is the only place a new kind cannot be added without passing. **Both oracles are runtime or structural, never a list of names.** The degradation proof boots a live analytics-only tenant, runs every Contact Center `IReport`, and requires each one declaring an unmet capability to return a single section that names the missing feature identifier and carries no rows, metrics, bars or chart — a live tenant because a report registered without the guard, or a guard registered in the wrong feature, still compiles and still returns zeroes. It fails as vacuous if nothing was degraded, so emptying the requirement map cannot make it pass quietly, and a third assertion fails if enabling analytics activates `Voice` or `Recording` at all. The provenance proof reflects over the persisted members of `Interaction` and `CallSession` and fails any member the report sources read that no production source outside the reports assigns or mutates — the only oracle that separates an empty measurement from a field nothing has ever populated, and the one that found both dead reports. **Review found the whole-report guard insufficient and it is fixed rather than documented around.** Guarding only the reports whose *entire* subject is voice or recording left the exact harm the item describes in place elsewhere: the flagship executive dashboard still published `Recording coverage: 0%` and `Transfer rate: 0%` as headline metrics, the agent volume and outcome reports still carried `Transfers`, `Recorded` and `Recording coverage` columns, the queue, agent, channel and daily usage reports still carried `Transfers` and `Recordings`, and interaction and exception detail still carried `Provider` and `Transfers` — all structural zeroes on a tenant that never had the capability. Withholding those reports would be wrong, because their primary figures are real work; the fix is to degrade at the granularity of the claim rather than the report, so the absent capability's columns and metrics are dropped from the layout while the rest of the report runs. A single per-layout requirement list drives the columns and every row including the grand total, so a column and its cells cannot drift apart, and a length mismatch throws rather than silently shifting a row. The gate was extended to match: a fourth assertion runs every report on the analytics-only tenant and fails if any column, metric or bar heading belongs to an absent capability. That assertion caught a real off-by-one in the first implementation (the usage layout declared seven requirements for eight columns). Falsified with 6 probes, 6 detected: reading an unwritten field from a report (caught, and the paired control — the same field with a writer added elsewhere in `src` — passes, so the oracle discriminates rather than rejecting all new members); removing the guard call from the enterprise provider; dropping `IContactCenterCapabilityDependentReport` from the workforce provider; adding `Voice`/`Recording` back to the `Analytics` manifest, which fails both the independence assertion and the vacuity assertion at once; and rendering the usage report’s columns unfiltered, which fails the column-level assertion.

The audit found the item was worse than it read: exactly one recipe step existed in the whole Contact Center module and no deployment step at all, and seven of the eight entity handlers never read `context.Data`, so a recipe that created a skill or a queue produced an entry with no name and no settings while reporting success. Rather than hand-write thirty-odd near-identical types, a generic configuration-catalog kit was added to `CrestApps.OrchardCore.Core` (`IConfigurationCatalog`, `ConfigurationCatalog<T>`, `ConfigurationCatalogEntryBinder`, one recipe step, and a group-filtered deployment step, source and editor base), and export/import are now driven by reflection over the entry type, so a property added to an entity later travels without anyone remembering to update a step. Scope was extended to the CRM catalogs the plan names alongside Contact Center configuration - dispositions, channel endpoints, campaign groups, campaigns, subject flows and subject actions - because a Contact Center tenant cannot be reproduced without the vocabulary it routes and reports on. Provider credentials are deliberately exempt: they are options-bound so that a plan committed to source control never carries a secret, and that exemption is stated in the operator documentation. Six sabotage probes were designed and six were detected, but only after the oracle was rewritten: the first probe - dropping `Description` from the export - was NOT detected, because comparing an export from one tenant against an export from another is satisfied by a step that drops the same property on both sides. The oracle now reads both tenants' entries straight from the managers that own them, and the probe is detected. Two further defects were found by the new gates rather than by review: the coverage gate caught `SubjectAction`, an entity nobody had decided about, and the identity gate caught that an import minted fresh identifiers while configuration references configuration by identifier, so every cross-reference in a plan landed on the destination pointing at nothing. Imports now keep the exported identifier, and the standard agent state reason codes the migrations seed carry fixed identifiers instead of each tenant minting its own. The headless-closure gate from W11.1 then caught the new deployment editors being registered in capability features, so the display drivers moved to the `.Admin` features while the step and source stay headless.  A second review pass against the finished code found nine further defects, all fixed before the item was closed. Agent profiles were withdrawn from configuration entirely: a profile names the person who holds it, carries their contact details, and records the state that person is in right now, so exporting one moved a person and their live presence between environments; it is declared runtime state instead. Reconciling an entry by name was found to be only half a fix - the destination keeps the identifier it had already published, and the rest of the plan still names the source's, so a plan replayed into a tenant that was already configured landed a contact centre that looked configured and routed nothing. Substitutions are now recorded for the length of one import and carried into the steps that follow, which also removes the upgrade caveat: tenants seeded before the reason-code identifiers were fixed are reconciled by name and their references repointed. Five further fixes followed: cleared values now travel instead of being omitted, values the owning manager derives are no longer overwritten by the plan's raw value, an entry is validated before it is stored rather than after, one unusable entry no longer aborts the step, and entries identified by display text rather than by a name - campaigns, campaign groups, channel endpoints, subject flows and subject actions - are reconciled instead of duplicated. Two of those fixes shipped initially with no gate that could see them: probes that reverted the display-text matching and the cleared-value export both passed, so three live-tenant cases and three direct catalog cases were added until every one of the six new probes was detected. Registering the identity store as an `IRecipeEventHandler` was found to terminate the tenant shell during feature activation; it is a self-evicting singleton instead. A third review pass found four more, and they were the ones that mattered most: reconciliation had been treated as a forward-only problem. A queue references a channel endpoint that a different deployment step carries and overflows into a queue in its own step, so no ordering of a plan makes every reference resolvable at the moment it is written, and an inbound number would have stopped reaching its queue on a tenant that looked configured. Substitutions are now applied to the entries already stored as well as to the entries still to come, after every step, which makes the import independent of the order an operator added the steps. Subject flow settings and subject actions were being reconciled on a display text that nothing in the product ever fills in, so every replay would have created a second copy and the product would have acted on both - the effective flow for a subject becoming whichever copy was read first, and a duplicated action running twice for one disposition; a catalog can now declare the members that identify its entries, and those two declare the subject, the disposition and the source. A hand-written plan that invented its own identifiers had them silently discarded and its cross-references left dangling; the invented identifier is now translated wherever the plan used it. The first attempt at a coverage gate for the third of these passed under sabotage, because the fixture populates every writable member and so filled in the very display text the product leaves empty - it was replaced with a case that creates the configuration the way the product creates it. A fourth review pass found two more: reconciling by name matched entries the plan itself had just created, so a plan carrying two entries under one name - two queues called "Support", or several subject actions on one disposition, both of which the product allows and neither of which any handler forbids - collapsed into one entry and silently redirected every reference to the one that was lost; each entry the destination already owned is now claimed once. And a step whose collection was named something the tenant did not recognise imported nothing and was reported as executed, which is the exact failure a plan exists to prevent, and was also a regression against the hand-written step this change replaced, since the recipe engine binds its own steps without regard to case; the collection is now matched without regard to case and a step that carries none of the configuration it can import is reported as an error. Eleven sabotage probes were run against the finished code and all eleven were detected.
- [x] W11.6 Voice webhook body bounded by what arrives `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test` — `RequestBodyReaderTests` (9), `ProviderVoiceWebhookEndpointTests` (7) and `DialPadWebhookEndpointTests` (13). The 1 MiB ceiling was checked against the content length the caller declares, and a caller that wants to send more than it is allowed to simply omits the header, so a chunked body was bounded only by whatever the host happened to allow and was then read into a string in one go. The body is now read through a shared bounded reader in `CrestApps.OrchardCore.Core` that measures what actually arrives and refuses it the moment it passes the allowance, before it is ever turned into a string; the same allowance is handed to the server through `IHttpMaxRequestBodySizeFeature` so the host can stop those bytes before they reach this process, and the server's own refusal is normalised to the same result so the three endpoints behave identically. The same reader replaced the unbounded read in the Azure Event Grid endpoint. The first attempt also moved the read ahead of the work lease and the ingress permit, on the reasoning that a slow caller should not occupy a permit while it uploads. Review found that trade to be the wrong way round twice over. Reading before the permit removes the only bound on how many bodies the process buffers at once - the permit limit is what keeps concurrent buffering to eight, and Kestrel's maximum concurrent connections is unlimited by default - while the slow caller it was meant to defend against is already handled by the server's minimum request body data rate. The leases are taken first again, and the gate now asserts the opposite property: when the concurrency limit is exhausted the endpoint refuses without reading a single byte of the body. Review also found a defect the tests could not have caught: the reader asked the pipe for more data without consuming what it had already been given. `DefaultHttpContext` exposes a stream-backed pipe with no pause threshold, but the server feeds a chunked body through a pipe that pauses its writer until the reader consumes, so every non-empty chunked request would have hung until the connection was aborted. The reader now consumes each buffer as it copies it, and a back-pressured pipe double stands in for the server so the gate can see it. Seven sabotage probes were run against the finished code - dropping the arriving-bytes ceiling, decoding only the first buffer, asking for more without consuming, dropping the server-refusal normalisation, reverting the endpoint to read before the leases, shifting the allowance boundary by one byte, and decoding each piece as it arrives instead of the body as a whole - and all seven were detected. The last two gates came from review: the boundary is now pinned from both sides, and a body whose pieces split a multi-byte character is fed through a back-pressured pipe seven bytes at a time so a per-piece decode substitutes characters the caller never sent.
- [x] W11.7 Write-path rules out of display drivers `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test` — `ValidationOwnershipArchitectureTests` (4), `CatalogEntryValidationTests` (8) and the five per-handler rule suites (`DialerProfileHandlerValidationTests`, `ActivityQueueHandlerValidationTests`, `SubjectFlowSettingsHandlerValidationTests`, `AISubjectFlowSettingsHandlerValidationTests`, `SubjectActionHandlerValidationTests`) plus `OmnichannelChannelEndpointHandlerCanonicalizationTests` (5); full suite 3,307 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped, activation 63 passed / 2 skipped, distributed 16 passed / 1 unchanged Redis-backplane failure. The two write paths enforced disjoint rule sets. `ConfigurationCatalog.ImportEntryAsync` calls the manager's `ValidateAsync` and aborts on failure, so a recipe ran only the handler rules; the admin controllers called `UpdateEditorAsync` and then saved on `ModelState.IsValid` without ever calling `ValidateAsync`, so the editor ran only the driver rules — and `CatalogManager<T>` does not validate on create or update. Every rule a display driver held for a configuration catalog entry has moved into that entry's handlers, which every write path runs, and the controllers now reach those handlers through `CatalogEntryValidation.ValidateAsync` between `UpdateEditorAsync` and the `ModelState` check, keyed to the same `"{Prefix}.{member}"` names the drivers used so the editor still highlights the field that is wrong. The call sits in the controller rather than in a driver because driver execution follows registration order and a feature-gated second driver for the same entity binds its fields after the first one runs; the controller is the only point at which every driver has finished binding. `SubjectFlowSettings` and `SubjectAction` had no handler at all, so a recipe could store either with no validation whatsoever; both now have one, and the AI-specific flow rules live in a separately registered handler gated by the same feature as the driver they came from. Two defects were fixed rather than carried: the channel-endpoint driver canonicalised phone numbers to E.164 while the recipe path stored them verbatim, so a recipe-written endpoint would never have matched inbound traffic — canonicalisation moved to the handler — and the same driver dereferenced a null value while trimming it. The dialer driver's three silent `Math.Clamp` calls were deleted rather than moved: clamping told the operator nothing and left the recipe path storing the value unclamped, so the range is now stated as a rule that fails with a message. The gate derives its governed set from the `AddConfigurationCatalog<,>` registrations themselves rather than from an allowlist, so a new configuration catalog is covered the moment it is registered; runtime aggregates that no recipe authors (`OmnichannelActivity`, `OmnichannelActivityBatch`, `Interaction`, `CallSession`, `QueueItem`, `AgentSession`) are out of scope by construction, as are site settings such as `ContactCenterRecordingSettings` and `DialPadSettings`, which a recipe writes through a settings step and which need a different fix shape. Two regressions the new rules exposed were fixed rather than suppressed: injecting the queue group manager into the queue handler closed a container cycle through the queue group handler, so it is resolved lazily with the reason recorded on the type; and the portability seeder was manufacturing entries that no rule would accept — a queue pointing at a queue group that did not exist and a dialer profile in a mode the product refuses — so it now points references at the identifiers the earlier step actually produced and overrides the generated values that the rules genuinely reject. **Review found three real defects and all three were fixed rather than documented around.** (1) Moving canonicalisation to `InitializingAsync`/`UpdatingAsync` traded the recipe hole for an editor hole: an editor builds a new entry before it binds the form to it, so the value is still empty when the entry is initialized, and a create raises only `Creating` — so an endpoint typed into the editor was stored exactly as typed and, since inbound matching is an exact comparison, would never have matched a call. Canonicalisation now also runs on `CreatingAsync`, which every create path raises, and five cases pin it. (2) The two new handlers were registered in the module's admin feature while the catalogs and recipe steps for the same entities are registered in the Activities feature, which the manifest documents as usable without any administration screens — so on an Activities-only tenant subject flows and subject actions would still have imported with nothing validating them. The registrations moved, and the gate now resolves the `Feature` attribute of the startup class that carries each registration - through the repository's own constants, falling back to the module identifier when a class carries no attribute - and requires every handler for a governed entity to be registered by the same feature that registers its catalog. (3) The portability seed overrides had been set to values that happen to be the type's defaults, so if the export had dropped `Mode` or `CallsPerAgent` entirely both tenants would have read back the default and the comparison would still have passed; they are now set to accepted values that differ from the defaults. Review also named three ways the gates could be walked around and all three are closed: the editor gate now reasons per action rather than per file, so an action that writes through the manager without updating an editor at all — a clone, a rename, a bulk toggle — is caught, while an action whose create and update branches share one validation is not falsely accused; the driver gate considers every `DisplayDriver<>` a file declares rather than only the first; and the declaration-site skip is anchored to the extension method's own declaration, so a registration written inside a static helper is still discovered. **A third review found four more real defects and all four were fixed.** (1) One rule had been tightened rather than moved: the driver only required a *named* subject to be configured, while the handler required a subject at all - but an empty subject is a supported, documented configuration that makes the new activity keep the subject type of the activity that raised it, which the editor offers as an option and the executor implements, so the tightening would have refused entries the product creates and broken the replay of any older deployment plan carrying one. (2) The gate resolved constants by their immediate declaring type only, and `Feature.Area` is declared by ten different constants classes with ten different values, so seven attributes in the repository - two of them in the very file that registers the Contact Center catalogs - resolved to another module's feature, which would have let a catalog and a handler in genuinely different features compare equal. Constants are now keyed by their full nesting path, an expression that still matches more than one value is left unresolved rather than guessed, and the gate fails if any governed registration resolves to something that is not a feature identifier. (3) The project fallback split the relative path on the platform separator while the paths are normalised to `/`, so on Windows every unattributed registration would have become its own feature and the gate would have reported violations that do not exist. (4) One portability seed override was still the type's default after the previous fix - `DialerMode.Manual` is the first enum member - so that property's round-trip assertion was vacuous; it is now a non-default mode the rules accept. Falsified with 10 probes, 10 detected: returning one rule to a display driver, deleting one rule from a handler, dropping one controller's validation call, removing one handler registration, adding a save action that writes through the manager with no editor update and no validation, moving a handler registration to a different feature from its catalog, removing the create-path canonicalisation, moving a handler between two feature-attributed startup classes in the same file, returning the AI flow handler to the administration feature, and moving a handler into an unattributed startup class so it falls to the module's default feature.
- [x] W11.8 Public API baseline approved `gate:pr_ci.yml#build_test` — `PublicApiApprovalTests` (33 executed cases across 8 governed assemblies); unit suite 3,372 passed / 0 failed / 1 skipped, activation 63 passed, distributed 16 passed / 1 failed (Redis backplane, no broker locally), strict Release build 0 warnings, docs build SUCCESS. **This row subsumes the forward reference W10.5 wrote to `gate:gate-public-api-approved`, which did not exist at the time; that gate is implemented here and both rows are bound to the job that runs it.** Everything these assemblies expose publicly is a promise to whoever compiles against them, and they are compiled against by other modules in this repository and by whatever a deployment builds beside them. The generated surface of each governed assembly is now checked in under `tests/CrestApps.OrchardCore.Tests/PublicApi/Baselines`, so a type turning public, a member changing shape, a class losing `sealed` or a parameter changing type arrives as a diff a reviewer accepts on purpose rather than as an ordinary-looking edit whose first bug report comes from a deployment that no longer builds. **Which assemblies are governed is derived rather than listed.** A hand-written list is a list somebody has to remember to add to, and the assembly nobody remembers is the one that breaks: the set is computed from the project graph, where a project in the Contact Center, Telephony or Omnichannel families becomes governed the moment a project that is not the packaging target or the web host compiles against it. That rule, not an opinion, is what widened the scope from the four Abstractions/Core contracts first considered to eight — it pulled in the `Telephony`, `Telephony.Core`, `Omnichannel` and `Omnichannel.Managements` module assemblies, which other modules genuinely reference at compile time, and it correctly left out `ContactCenter`, `Omnichannel.Sms` and `Omnichannel.EventGrid`, which nothing compiles against. The derivation is guarded against collapsing in either direction: it fails if no family project is found, if none is consumed, or if every one of them is, which would mean it had stopped telling contracts apart from leaf modules. **The audit itself found the surface already disciplined and one thing that was not.** Across the eight assemblies there are 379 sealed classes, 164 interfaces, 68 static classes, 64 enums and 4 abstract classes — every one of the abstract classes an intentional `*Base` extension point — and no public static field that anything can reassign. It did not, on the first pass, find the shared mutable state described under (3) below, because the rule as first written asked only whether a reference could be reassigned. **Because a recorded surface is still only text, and text is easy to accept in bulk, the audit's conclusions are also stated as rules** so that breaking one arrives as a named failure rather than as one more line in a diff someone is scrolling through: a public class must be sealed unless it is abstract, introduces something overridable, or is a view model, and no public type may expose static state that anything in the process can change. **Writing that rule as "must be sealed" would have been wrong, and the first run proved it.** It flagged 32 classes, and reading them rather than sealing them mattered: 31 are view models, which the display framework has to build a runtime proxy from and therefore cannot seal, and the 32nd, `DefaultContactActivityBatchLoader`, is documented in `docs/omnichannel/management.md` as deliberately inheritable so a custom loader can reuse its contact-paging pipeline. Sealing either group would have broken working, documented behaviour to satisfy a gate. The rule now separates intent from omission — a class that *introduces* a `virtual` member is inviting derivation, a view model is unsealed because the framework requires it, and anything else unsealed is unsealed because nobody typed the keyword — which is the case actually worth failing on. **Review found five real defects and all five were fixed rather than documented around.** (1) **The gate could not have passed on any machine but the one that wrote it.** OrchardCore emits one `ModuleAsset` attribute per view carrying the absolute path it was compiled from, and PublicApiGenerator records assembly attributes, so three baselines contained this clone's directory layout - 134 `ModuleAsset` and 118 `RazorCompiledItem` lines that also meant editing any `.cshtml` produced a public-surface diff. On CI the gate would have been red on the first run with overwriting the baseline the only way to clear it, which is precisely the unread bulk acceptance it exists to prevent. Those two attributes are excluded, and because the next attribute to carry a path will not be on that list, a recorded surface containing a filesystem path now fails on its own. (2) **The sealing rule accepted overriding a member as evidence of intent.** In IL an `override` is virtual and not final, so "declares something overridable" was implemented as "declares or overrides", which any display driver satisfies with a single `public override`, and every public record satisfies for free through its synthesized equality members - the rule could never have fired on a record. A method now counts only when this type is where it becomes virtual, and compiler-synthesized members are excluded. (3) **The static-state rule checked only that a reference could not be reassigned, and the governed set contained exactly the hazard it missed.** `InteractionStatuses.OccupyingAgent`, `.Unsettled` and `.Settled` were `public static readonly` arrays read directly by the interaction store's query predicates; any code in the process could assign to an element and permanently change what counts as occupying an agent for every tenant. `TelephonyCapabilityContracts.ContractsByCapability` was a `Dictionary` handed out behind `IReadOnlyDictionary` that a caller could cast back and edit. Both were fixed at the source - `ImmutableArray` and `FrozenDictionary` - and the rule now judges the value a member actually holds rather than the type it is declared as, asking the instance whether it refuses modification and rejecting arrays outright because they report themselves read-only while still allowing element assignment. Judging the value rather than the declaration is also what keeps it honest in the other direction: `ContactCenterTopologyProfiles.All` is declared as a read-only interface but is really a frozen collection, and it passes. (4) **The failure diff compared line sets, so about half of every baseline was invisible to it** - `public long DocumentId { get; set; }` alone appears more than twenty times in one file - meaning deleting one of those members reported "the surface no longer matches" with nothing listed underneath, and a reviewer who cannot see what changed accepts the file unread. Lines are now qualified by their enclosing type and subtracted by occurrence. (5) **A newly governed assembly the test project did not reference would have thrown out of the `MemberData` provider**, aborting every case in the class with a file-not-found instead of asking for a baseline; the data provider no longer loads anything and assemblies are resolved from the test output by file, so the failure names the missing project reference. Falsified with 11 probes, 11 detected: leaking a new public type into a governed assembly (fails the baseline with the added lines named), that same type being unsealed with nothing to override (fails the sealing rule), that same type holding a public static field (fails the static-state rule), deleting a baseline (fails and rewrites it to be read and committed), leaving a baseline behind for an assembly nothing compiles against (fails as orphaned), adding a cross-module project reference to a previously ungoverned family project (which immediately demanded a baseline for it, proving the governed set is derived and not decorative), an unsealed public class whose only virtual member is an override of a base one (2), an unsealed public record (2), a `public static readonly IReadOnlyList<string>` backed by a `List<string>` (3), and a filesystem path planted in a recorded baseline (1). The line-qualified diff (4) was observed directly in the output of the first three of those probes, which named the enclosing type of every changed line.

One database takes the fresh-installation path, which is the create step **followed by every update step Orchard still applies afterwards** — modelling a fresh install as the create step alone was the first thing this harness got wrong, and it reported two real columns as missing. The other is installed at the previous schema version and then upgraded: where a fresh install still runs an update step, the previous version is the same chain stopped one step short, so nothing is synthesised; where the create step already reports the current version, the update step is the only surviving description of what the older version lacked, so the older table is the current one minus the columns that step adds. A previous-version writer and a current-version writer then both insert into the **upgraded** tables and the previous version's projection is read back, which is the only state a rolling upgrade actually produces. A further assertion compares every column definition and every unique constraint between the two databases. **This gate found a real defect rather than confirming a belief:** the reservation and queue-item claim keys were declared with an inline unique constraint and no default on the create path but with a named unique index and an empty-string default on the upgrade path, so the same release produced two different schemas depending on when the tenant was installed, and only the upgraded one could accept a previous-version write. The create steps now build the constraints exactly the way the upgrade path builds them. Falsified with 4 probes: breaking migration discovery (all 4 fail), adding a default in an update step that the create step lacks (convergence only), dropping a column in an update step (convergence and the previous-version write), and adding a non-nullable column with no default — the headline case the static additive-migration gate cannot catch, which fails with `NOT NULL constraint failed` on the previous-version write exactly as the harness promises. One hazard is recorded as an operator constraint rather than enforced, because no portable fix exists in a single release: an upgrade that adds a non-nullable column with a shared default and then constrains it uniquely admits only one previous-version write, since every previous-version node writes the same default. Filtered indexes are not portable across the supported engines and nullable columns do not help, because not every engine treats nulls as distinct; the supported answer is to expand and contract across two releases.

## 14. Independent challenge and consensus (2026-07-26)

This plan was challenged by an independent reviewer on a different model family, given repo access and instructed to find what the plan fails to close. Its verdict on the plan as written was **"No — does not produce a production-ready platform"**. Every claim below was independently verified against the code before acceptance. Findings 1, 6 and the erasure finding are defects **in this plan**, not merely in the product.

### Accepted — plan corrected in place

1. **W1.1 was architecturally impossible.** Corrected above. `ProviderVoiceEventService` carries 9 Contact Center-specific dependencies; moving it wholesale into `Telephony.Core` would have inverted the layering. Now split into provider-neutral ingress mechanics plus a Contact Center projection, with shadow-replay cutover.
2. **W3.1's lease key would have caused cross-tenant event leakage.** Corrected above. Tenant must stay ownership *metadata*, never part of the key.
3. **Sequencing contradictions.** The risk table said "ship the W8.5 reset tool first" while scheduling it in Wave 8; W1's mitigation named ARI cassettes and property tests that were scheduled four waves later; W15.3 (N-1 proof) landed after the W2 breaking migrations it exists to protect. **Resolved in §6:** W5.4 cassettes and W5.6 property tests move to Wave 2 as W1 entry criteria; W8.5 reset tooling and W15.2/W15.3 move to Wave 1 as W2 entry criteria. **A breaking data change may not merge before the tooling that makes it recoverable.**
4. **W15.2's destructive-migration ban needs an explicit contract-step exception**, otherwise it forbids the very "contract" phase of the expand-migrate-contract policy W2 depends on. The gate must permit destructive steps only when accompanied by a declared, reviewed contract-phase marker. **Resolved in W15.2:** the register carries a `ContractPhase` justification that is accepted only when the object was introduced in a strictly older release, so the contract phase is permitted while expand-and-contract-in-one-release remains impossible.
5. **Track A positioning must be stated, not implied.** Track A is a voice-only ACD for customers explicitly accepting no omnichannel, no proficiency/bullseye routing, no virtual hold, and no WFM/QM. All language implying parity with Genesys/NICE/Five9/Amazon Connect is removed. §12 already says this; §1 must not contradict it in marketing terms.
6. **W10.6 (open channel model) is scope creep — deferred to Track B.** The justification was "avoid a second breaking change", but breaking changes are permitted pre-GA, so that is not sufficient reason to build a generic extension system before a single concrete channel exists to inform its routing, capacity, reporting, retention and consent requirements. Removed from Wave 2; moves to B3 as the first task of the first channel vertical slice.

### Accepted — new work added

7. **W17 — Subject erasure and media lifecycle (BLOCKING for the `recording` capability).** The single most serious product finding of the entire review, missed by all eight specialists and by the first challenge. `IRecordingAccessGovernanceService.EraseAsync` clears the interaction pointer, stamps `RecordingErasedUtc` and emits a `RecordingErased` event (`RecordingAccessGovernanceService.cs:112-141`) — but a repository-wide search finds **zero callers of `EraseAsync` outside its own definition, and zero consumers of the `RecordingErased` event.** The encrypted media store does expose deletion (`LocalEncryptedRecordingMediaStore.cs:81-102`), and nothing calls it. Separately, retention purges **only** `InteractionEvent` rows (`ContactCenterRetentionService.cs:23-49`) and never the media referenced by `RecordingRetainUntilUtc`. **Net effect: recorded call audio is never deleted, by any path, ever.** GDPR Article 17, CCPA deletion, and every contractual retention commitment are currently unimplementable. Required: an authenticated erasure API and workflow that calls `EraseAsync`; a durable media-deletion command routed through the outbox with retry and reconciliation; a retention sweeper that deletes expired media and honours legal hold; transcript erasure; tenant-decommission cleanup; a deletion receipt in the audit trail; and an integration test proving the encrypted bytes are gone from the store.
8. **W18 — Configuration validation, fail-closed.** Retention and health options are registered with bare `Configure<T>` and no validation (`ContactCenter/Startup.cs:72-90`). Add `IValidateOptions<T>` with `ValidateOnStart` for every Contact Center, Telephony and provider options class, and a production startup validator that **refuses to start** on known-development values — including the checked-in Coturn development secret `static-auth-secret=crestapps-dev-turn-secret` (`Coturn/turnserver.conf:8`). Externalize hard-coded timing and lease values.
9. **W12.12 — Signed origination markers.** `AsteriskRealtimeVoiceEventMapper.cs:43-47` infers origination ownership from the mere *presence* of a channel variable, with no signature. Anything able to set that variable can forge ownership. Replace with an HMAC over tenant, call and command identity, verified before ownership is accepted. This is the correct closure of telephony 4.5, which W12 claimed but did not own.
10. **W12.13 — Durable pre-buffer event journal.** Telephony 4.2 is not closed by reconciliation: reconciliation recovers *current* state but cannot reconstruct the intermediate Hold/Resume sequence lost when the bounded channel saturates. Journal normalized events durably *before* the bounded channel, account for overflow explicitly, and gate on zero lifecycle loss under induced saturation.
11. **W5.4/W5.5 must cover DialPad, not only Asterisk.** DialPad is a supported provider profile; contract and reconciliation tests currently stop at Asterisk cassettes. **W5.4 half discharged** — `DialPadWebhookContractTests` binds the DialPad webhook to recorded deliveries replayed through the signed ingress, the production deserializer and the production normalizer, with source-scanned coverage floors over every provider token the normalizer interprets. The guarantee is deliberately weaker than Asterisk's and is declared as such: DialPad publishes no vendorable schema, so its manifest records the contract as payload-bound rather than specification-bound. W5.5 remains open.
12. **W9.1/W12.4 — DialPad timestamp parsing is timezone-unsafe.** `DateTimeOffset.TryParse(value.GetString(), out var parsed)` (`DialPadTelephonyProvider.cs:966`) supplies neither `CultureInfo.InvariantCulture` nor `DateTimeStyles.AssumeUniversal | AdjustToUniversal`, so an offset-less provider timestamp is interpreted in the **host's** local timezone — corrupting call duration and report bucketing, and doing so differently on either side of a DST boundary. Require offset-bearing timestamps or parse with explicit universal styles; test both DST boundaries.
13. **W0.5 must include container image scanning** (Trivy/Grype) for the Asterisk image; the task listed SBOM, secret scanning and license inventory but omitted it. *(Resolved in W0.5: `supply_chain.yml#container-scan`.)*
14. **W0.4 — docs validation must run on code PRs**, not only doc-path PRs, or code changes silently invalidate documented claims. *(Resolved in W0.4: `validate_docs.yml` now triggers on `src/**` and `tests/**`.)*
15. **Legacy inbound endpoint disposition (orchard F-11)** must be named explicitly: sunset or rename it, and require a strict E.164-or-ambiguous routing result rather than a best-effort match.

### Accepted — evidence model strengthened

16. **A workflow job name is not evidence.** W0.3 only proved that a ticked checkbox referenced an *existing* job — not that the job tests the claim. That is RC-3 recurring one level up. **New rule (supersedes AD-6):** every gate requires a versioned test specification stating topology, inputs and injected faults, the invariant asserted, the observation source, numerical pass thresholds, and prohibited mocks/skips. `gate-ledger-evidence` validates that each gate has a specification and that the specification's thresholds are the ones the job actually asserts.
17. **Blank gate values are now release-blocking.** ~20 ledger entries in §13 carry `gate:` with no value. Any entry without a named gate and specification cannot be ticked.
18. **Named-but-unspecified gates must be quantified:** `gate-capacity` (duration, workload mix, error budget, p95 ceiling, minimum retained capacity), W2.3's "5M rows return to steady state" (hardware, distribution, runtime, rate), W5.7's "publish p95" (thresholds, not just publication), and the audio proofs (unique per-leg stimuli, channel-mapping validation, real provider path — a file-existence assertion must not pass).
19. **`gate-crm-review-closed` must not be satisfiable by accepting every finding.** Risk acceptance requires a named independent reviewer and a dated, written rationale per accepted finding.
20. **Capacity caps need a commercial floor.** §2.3 says to lower published caps to measured values, with no lower bound — a system could "pass" at 5 agents. Define the minimum viable commercial capacity below which the release does not ship.

### Rejected / retained as-is

- **Keep the Telephony module as a standalone SKU.** Re-confirmed by both challenges.
- **Instrument after the seams stabilize (AD-5).** Re-confirmed; instrumenting duplicate stacks first would institutionalize identifiers that W1 then reworks.
- **Track A before Track B.** Re-confirmed as correct engineering: hardening authority and persistence before multiplying channel surface is precisely the discipline whose absence produced RC-1. The challenge agreed this ordering must not be reversed.
- **One application node cannot earn a 10/10 scalability score.** Re-confirmed against `support-matrix.v1.json:29-47`.
